a mathematical modelling study

Gavin J Haynes, Nicholas G White, Adam J Trickey, Michael J Quail, Robert J Williams, Roderick J Haynes

Keywords: Mathematical modelling; Epidemiology; Virus; SARS-CoV-2; COVID-19; Zambia

Background

Zambia has experienced a rapid increase in COVID-19 cases since March 2020. On 3 April 2020, 24 confirmed cases were reported by the national COVID-19 committee, but by 11 June 2020 this had increased to 1040 confirmed cases. The Lusaka health provincial authority declared a 14-day lockdown of the entire province on 15 April 2020. The lockdown was partially lifted on 3 June 2020.

Methods We developed a mathematical model to assess the impact of a blanket testing strategy on the control of the COVID-19 outbreak in Lusaka, Zambia. The model considers three different testing strategies that incorporate the impact of asymptomatic individuals. The model also considers the 14-day lockdown period and reduces the mixing parameter to account for reduced contact rates during this period. Parameter values are taken from the literature or calculated from age-specific survival data from the Zambia 2010 Demographic and Health Survey. Parameter values are assumed to be constant during the course of the outbreak.

Results For a lockdown period with no testing, the final size of the outbreak is estimated to be 4.06 million individuals with 19 460 (0.48%) deaths. With no lockdown and no testing, the final size of the outbreak is estimated to be 7.16 million individuals with 63 172 (1.77%) deaths. Comparing the different testing strategies during the lockdown period, testing all individuals with a 1% false negative rate is optimal with a final outbreak size of 1.12 million individuals with 11 400 (0.32%) deaths. This strategy outperforms strategies that test only those with symptoms or only those randomly selected for testing.

Conclusions The modelling results indicate that implementation of a blanket testing strategy in Lusaka, Zambia during the lockdown period would have significantly reduced the number of cases and deaths from the COVID-19 outbreak. The findings also highlight the need for increased COVID-19 related investment in Zambia, particularly in strengthening the existing health system.

However, the role of asymptomatic infection in the spread of COVID-19 in Africa is not well understood. Here, we review the evidence on asymptomatic infection in Africa and discuss the implications for testing and contact tracing strategies. Given the limited resources in most African countries, a strategy that identifies only symptomatic individuals for testing and treats or isolates them may be the most feasible strategy for now. However, the current evidence suggests that asymptomatic infection is not rare in Africa and that a substantial proportion of transmission may be driven by such individuals. This suggests that a strategy that also includes testing or tracing of contacts of asymptomatic individuals is needed to comprehensively understand the dynamics of the COVID-19 pandemic in African countries.

In this study, we characterized the presence, diversity and anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity of faecal microbiota in COVID-19 patients.
We analysed 203 faecal samples collected from COVID-19 patients, during hospitalisation. Faecal samples were assessed for the presence of bacteria known to be active against SARS-CoV-2, as well as for the presence of bacterial virulence factors and fungal metabolites with anti-viral activities.
We identified several anti-SARS-CoV-2 active components in the faecal microbiota of patients, including short chain fatty acids, bacterial secreted peptides, and fungal metabolites. Anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity was mainly associated with members of the families Enterobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae, and the genus Faecalibacterium. We also demonstrated a negative correlation between the diversity of the faecal microbiota and the severity of the disease.
This study confirms that the faecal microbiota of patients with COVID-19 displays an anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity. These findings suggest that modulation of the gut microbiota may be an additional therapeutic approach to counteract SARS-CoV-2 infection.

The model was calibrated to the data from the first 40 days of the outbreak when the majority of cases were in the early stages of the disease. The model was then simulated for 80 days beyond the calibration period to predict the impact of the control strategy. The simulation results show that the outbreak can be controlled and the number of cases can be reduced by 95% if the infected but asymptomatic individuals are isolated for at least 7 days. However, if the infected but asymptomatic individuals are isolated for less than 7 days, the outbreak cannot be controlled and the number of cases can increase by 100%. The number of cases can be reduced by 60% if only symptomatic individuals are isolated for 14 days. The results from this study can be used by decision makers to develop effective control strategies for COVID-19 outbreaks in similar settings.

The R0 for SARS-CoV-2 in the USA and ROK are estimated to be 2.4 and 3.9, respectively . We assumed an effective contact number of 2.5, which is the average of the USA and ROK. The overall case fatality ratio (CFR) for SARS-CoV-2 is around 1.8%  and we assumed a 98% quarantine rate. The percentage of asymptomatic individuals was set at 70% for scenario 1 and 50% for scenario 2. The percentage of infected individuals who recovered was set at 80% for both scenarios, which is the average of the ROK and USA data. The remaining 20% of the infected individuals were assumed to be the COVID-19 positive cases requiring hospitalization. For both scenarios, we assumed that the infected individuals were evenly distributed across the entire population of each country, and the transmission occurred in all 50 states in the USA and 17 metropolitan areas in the ROK. The population of the USA and ROK used in the modelling were 330 million and 51 million, respectively. The model was run for 200 days, which was when the daily new cases stopped increasing in the ROK and USA.

The number of daily new cases for scenario 2 in the USA and ROK would start to decrease after 40 and 33 days, respectively, and the number of daily new cases would reduce to less than 1,000 for both countries after 200 days (Fig 2B). The required testing rates for the different scenarios were higher for the higher level of infectiousness. The results indicate that the impact of the proportion of asymptomatic individuals on the required testing rate to control the outbreak was significant. The lower the prevalence of symptoms, the higher the required testing rate. This is because asymptomatic individuals can spread the disease more efficiently than symptomatic individuals. Therefore, a higher testing rate is required to identify cases and to break chains of transmission. This study has some limitations. First, we estimated the reproduction number using the methodology of the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation which was validated for sub-Saharan Africa. However, the methodology might not be valid for South Africa. Second, we estimated the proportion of asymptomatic individuals based on a review of available evidence from China, Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, and the USA. However, given the rapid evolution of the pandemic, new evidence is emerging from different countries. Finally, the impact of the testing strategies on the required testing rate to control the outbreak was not considered in this study. Future studies should consider the impact of the testing strategies on the required testing rate to control the outbreak, using country-specific data. The findings of this study could be used to guide the development of strategies to control the COVID-19 pandemic. The Ministry of Health in Zambia has started a mass testing drive in Lusaka, the country's economic hub and largest city. But with only 4,680 tests conducted so far, critics say the exercise is futile.

The first COVID-19 case in Zambia was recorded on 18 March. Since then, the country has recorded 38 cases and one death. Both the confirmed cases and death are in Lusaka.

Mass testing in big cities like Lusaka may limit COVID-19 spread, but is it practical?

Zambian health officials say mass testing in Lusaka will help them to take swift action to contain the spread of the virus.

But critics say the mass testing is a futile exercise, given that the country has so far conducted only 4,680 tests, and most of the tests were done on people showing symptoms of the virus.

Zambian health experts say mass testing is the only way to quickly identify people who are infected with the virus.

Dr. Aaron Meja, a Zambian medical doctor who has been leading the fight against HIV/AIDS in the country for the past 20 years, says the mass testing strategy is the best way to contain the spread of the virus.

"Let's not be overburdened by the idea of testing. We have to be practical. If you are testing one person at a time, it will take you a long time to test a large number of people. But if you test 10 people at a time, you will be able to test a large number of people in a short period of time," he said.

Meja said the strategy of testing people in their homes will help to limit the movement of people, who could be infected with the virus.

But not everyone is in favor of the mass testing strategy. Some people in Lusaka say the strategy will not be effective in curbing the spread of the virus.

"I don't think it will help because the virus is spreading like fire right now. If you test people, you will just be able to isolate a few people," said one resident, who asked to be anonymous.

Another resident said it would have been better to screen people before they are allowed into the city.

"It would have been better to screen people before they come into Lusaka, at roadblocks, or even at the borders," the man said.

The recent advances in polygenic scores (PGS) have sparked a lot of interest in the use of complex genetic risk models for predicting disease risk. However, most of the studies that have contributed to these advances have been conducted in European populations. Therefore, it remains unclear to what extent PGS can be generalized to populations outside of Europe, and if they can provide accurate estimates of genetic risk in these populations. Here, we estimated the generalizability of PGS for 34 complex traits to 38 African populations using a meta-analysis approach. We then compared the generalizability of PGS across populations from different regions. We further evaluated the potential of PGS in risk prediction in African populations by developing PGS for type 2 diabetes in 38 African populations, and evaluating their performance in an independent African cohort. We observed low generalizability of PGS across African populations, due to both genetic and environmental heterogeneity between the populations. We also observed that the low generalizability of PGS is not limited to African populations as we also observed similar results for populations from other regions. These results suggest that there is a need to collect more data from diverse populations, and that PGS may not be generalizable to populations outside of Europe due to population structure and environmental differences. This may have important implications for the use of PGS in precision medicine, particularly in populations with limited data availability.

To investigate the impact of these factors on the genetic association of interest, we conducted a large meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of 34,400 individuals of African descent and compared our results with previously reported GWAS of European and South Asian populations. We identified 17 new loci (P < 5 × 10−8) in or near genes that were not reported previously in any GWAS and 100 known loci that were identified in GWAS of European and South Asian populations but not in smaller African GWAS. We also identified 66 loci that were unique to African populations. These loci are the combined effect of demography, environmental exposures, and selection that are unique to African populations. Our results suggest that a large proportion (>50%) of loci identified in the GWAS of European and South Asian populations may not have functional relevance in African populations. These findings will inform study design and fine-mapping efforts in African populations with the ultimate goal of improving disease prediction, prevention, and treatment in these populations.

We find that PRS for disease are strongly correlated with prior estimates of ancestry-specific genetic liability (R2 = 0.89), and that PRS explain similar amounts of phenotypic variance across different continents after accounting for ancestry (R2 = 0.16 in Africa, 0.17 in South America, and 0.21 in Europe). We also find that PRS capture more phenotypic variance than is explained by self-reported ancestry (R2 = 0.01 in Africa and 0.06 in the UK). These results suggest that polygenic scores derived and tested in one population can be generalized to populations with very different ancestry compositions, with small to moderate loss of accuracy. These findings have important implications for the interpretation of polygenic scores and may increase the cost-benefit profile of PRS-based risk prediction in understudied populations.

The UK sample is predominantly from West Africa, while the Uganda cohort is predominantly from East Africa. There are also small amounts of African ancestry in the UK cohort that is not found in the Uganda cohort, and vice versa, which could also contribute to the observed differences in PRS accuracy (Figure 2). This result highlights the importance of considering the geographic origin of African ancestry in PRS studies. It also suggests that African ancestry in the US, which is also predominantly from West Africa, would have a similar effect on PRS accuracy as seen in the UK cohort. This is further supported by a comparison of the UK and African American/Caribbean samples in the PGC SCZ consortium, which found no difference in PRS accuracy between these two cohorts (Online Supplementary Table 20). To further investigate the effect of the geographic origin of African ancestry on PRS accuracy, the UK African ancestry samples were separated into those with an East African or West African ancestral background. There was no significant difference in PRS accuracy between these two groups (p = 0.34, two-sided t-test, d = −0.10), suggesting that the geographic origin of African ancestry within the UK cohort does not contribute significantly to variability in PRS accuracy. This result should be interpreted with caution however, as the sample sizes for these comparisons were small (East African: n = 160; West African: n = 224).

samples.hyp:
The genetic basis of disease is not the same in different ethnic groups. Researchers are now using a combination of statistical and laboratory methods to better understand the genetic basis of disease in people of African ancestry.

Genetic testing is used to determine if someone is at risk of developing, or already has, a genetic disease. These tests can be very useful for people of European ancestry, where the genetic basis of many diseases has been well characterized. However, people of African ancestry are currently underrepresented in databases that are used to develop these tests. This means that people of African descent are often told that they are at “increased risk” or “at risk” of developing a disease, when in actual fact, the risk may be much lower or they may not be at risk at all. This can lead to unnecessary anxiety and high costs for genetic testing that may not be able to provide meaningful results for this population.

There are also many genetic variants (variants are differences) in the DNA that have the same effect on people of African descent, but are not present in people of other ethnicities. This further complicates the situation. In order to determine whether someone is at risk of developing a genetic disease, it is important to know which DNA changes (variants) are likely to have an impact on health. If these variants have not been characterized in the ethnic group of the person in question, the person will not receive an accurate genetic risk prediction.

The GENETRA project

The GENETRA project is a collaboration between scientists based in the UK, the USA, Kenya and Brazil, and involves multiple research groups and patient organisations. The aim of the project is to determine the genetic contribution of rare variants in common diseases in people of African ancestry. It is funded by the Wellcome Trust, and is led by Dr Eunice Fananje of the University of Oxford, UK, and Dr Laura James of the University of Cape Town, South Africa.

The project will characterise over 2,300 genetic variants that have been identified as being rare but potentially medically important in people of European descent. The team will also search for other variants that may have been missed by previous studies. The researchers will do this by collecting DNA samples from people in Kenya and Brazil, countries which have large populations of African descent, and which have been underrepresented in previous genetic research. The team will also collect health information from these individuals to determine whether any of these variants are associated with an increased risk of disease.

"Although the current COVID-19 vaccines are effective, the genetic data will be crucial for the development of future, improved vaccines," says Hugo Chazelle, first author of the study. "We are now for the first time combining high-resolution genetic data with information about the patients' medical history and treatment outcomes. This will allow us to identify signals that are specific for a certain disease and which can be used to develop better treatments."
The researchers used machine learning to analyze the data. The goal was to predict which patients would develop severe COVID-19 cases based on their genetic data alone. The results show that the model is able to predict which patients will develop severe disease with 78 percent accuracy. When including information about age and sex, the prediction was almost 90 percent accurate.
The researchers also wanted to investigate whether the genetic risk scores predicted which patients would need to be admitted to an ICU. The model predicted the correct patients with an accuracy of 80 percent. The researchers also tested whether the model could predict which patients would develop severe COVID-19 despite being vaccinated. The model predicted the correct patients in 85 percent of cases.
"Although it is not time to stop the research, it is still too early to use these models in practice. We still have many things to learn about the correlation between genes and COVID-19," says first author Hugo Chazelle. "But in the long run, this kind of model could be very useful. It could be combined with vaccination data, for example, to get a complete overview of the patients' risk of developing severe COVID-19."

This study evaluated the performance of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) with or without cervical cytology screening compared to cervical cytology screening alone for the detection of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer in Namibia.

A retrospective cohort study was conducted with Namibian women aged 30–49 years who had a cervical cytology screen and a VIA test as part of the cervical cancer screening program at one of three health facilities in the country between 2014 and 2017. The cytotechnology laboratory at the University of Namibia Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology was used for cytology testing and VIA was performed on site at each health facility by trained nurses. VIA was performed after cervical cytology screening and before cervical cytology reporting to allow for repeated examinations if the cytology result was inadequate. CIN lesions were treated according to national treatment guidelines. The primary outcome was the detection of CIN lesions and cervical cancer. The secondary outcome was to evaluate the predictive value of VIA in relation to the cervical cytology test result.

A total of 11,585 women had a cervical cytology screen and a VIA test. The mean age of the cohort was 37.8 years (standard deviation ± 6.1 years). Of these, 10,558 (91.8%) women had a normal cervical cytology result and 1,027 (8.2%) had an inadequate cervical cytology result. Among women with an inadequate cervical cytology result, 23.0% had an abnormal VIA result. Among women with a normal cervical cytology result, 3.1% had an abnormal VIA result. Of the 1,027 women with an inadequate cervical cytology result, 232 (22.6%) had a CIN lesion on histology and 98 (9.5%) had invasive cervical cancer. Among women with an abnormal VIA result, 16.0% had a CIN lesion on histology and 13.5% had invasive cervical cancer. The specificity and positive predictive value of VIA was 80.4% and 50.4%, respectively, when comparing VIA with cervical cytology.

VIA is a simple, non-invasive method for the detection of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN). Cryotherapy is a suitable treatment for low-grade CIN and AIN. The aim of this study was to evaluate the acceptance of VIA and cryotherapy in a low-resource setting in Côte d’Ivoire.
A prospective, non-randomized, clinical study of VIA and cryotherapy for the treatment of CIN and AIN was conducted in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. The primary outcome was the rate of acceptance of the combined intervention of VIA and cryotherapy. Secondary outcomes included the rate of acceptance of VIA and the rate of acceptance of cryotherapy.
Of 192 patients screened, 151 (79%) agreed to participate in the study. Of these, 126 (83%) were treated with VIA and cryotherapy, 17 (11%) with VIA only and 8 (5%) with cryotherapy only. Patient acceptance of VIA and cryotherapy was 96% and 100%, respectively. The study was terminated early due to low recruitment.
VIA and cryotherapy are two valuable tools in the management of cervical and anal neoplasia. VIA and cryotherapy were well accepted by the patients. This combined intervention is highly acceptable to women and should be further evaluated in low-resource countries.

We searched for randomised controlled trials, clinical effectiveness studies and cost-effectiveness analyses up to February 2018. Two reviewers independently screened and selected studies and extracted data. We performed meta-analyses for VIA compared to no screening and for ITC compared to VIA without ITC. A retrospective cohort study was conducted from June 2013 to June 2015 in the Central Region of Namibia. Data was extracted from medical records of patients aged 30–69 years. The primary outcome was cervical cancer and the occurrence of CIN was the secondary outcome. Chi-square and odds ratio were used for data analysis under the SPSS 2.0 software. There were 1256 women who had visual screening and 30.4% had return visits. 1020 women underwent visual and cytology screening and 22.0% had return visits. Visual screening detected 29 cases of CIN, cytology screening detected 13 cases and 16 cases were detected through the combination of both screening methods. Visual screening was 64.1% sensitive and 86.0% specific compared to cytology screening that was 100.0% sensitive and 97.3% specific. A significant difference existed between cytology and visual + cytology screening (p < 0.01). Visual screening combined with cytology is more effective in detecting cervical lesions than cytology or visual screening alone.

HPV is a common virus that affects many people, with the World Health Organization (WHO) estimating that two-thirds of men and women will be infected with HPV at some point in their lives. Cervical cancer is mostly caused by the human papillomavirus, with the WHO stating that 99% of cervical cancers are caused by HPV infection. This means that HPV vaccination is key to preventing cervical cancer.

While several countries in Africa have introduced national HPV vaccination programs, several others have yet to do so, with access to vaccination being a key factor as to why.

HPV vaccination in Africa

HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the world, with the WHO stating that there are more than 100 different strains of HPV.

Of these strains, some are low risk and cause no health consequences, while others are high risk and can cause cancer. Most cervical cancers are caused by two high-risk strains of HPV known as HPV16 and HPV18.

While the implementation of HPV vaccination programs has been slow, things are starting to look up. The WHO reports that no African country had implemented a national program when HPV vaccination was introduced on a global level in 2017.

The study used data from the UK’s National Cervical Screening Programme (NCSP), which changed from 5-yearly smears to 3-yearly smears for women aged 25-49 in 2008. 

The researchers used a mathematical model to look at the effects of different screening intervals and the accuracy of different tests. 

They found that using an 8-year screening interval, rather than the current 5 or 3-yearly screenings, and using a test which tests for HPV as well as changes to the cervix, would lead to the fewest number of life-saving procedures. 

Study author Professor Evelyn Graham, from the University of Aberdeen, said: “The current cervical screening programme in the UK is one of the best in the world, but we want to improve it even further. 

“This study shows that a new screening test which tests for HPV as well as changes to the cervix, and a longer 8-year screening interval, would result in more women having their condition diagnosed and treated, as well as fewer life-saving procedures.”

The researchers say that further trials are needed to test their proposed model in practice.

She had a 2-cm nodule of suspected hepatocellular carcinoma resected from the liver. Pathology confirmed hepatocellular carcinoma. These findings have important implications given the global distribution of HBV monoinfection and its overlap with HIV infection, especially in Africa and Asia, where HBV and HIV infection are highly coendemic. 

In our cohort, individuals with HBV monoinfection were significantly more likely to be younger, have a higher body mass index, have a higher frequency of HBV e-antigen positivity, and a lower frequency of cirrhosis or liver cancer at enrollment compared to those with HIV coinfection. These data suggest that individuals with HBV monoinfection are likely to be enrolled in care at earlier stages of disease than those with HIV coinfection. Earlier disease stage could explain why those with HBV monoinfection were less likely to have cirrhosis or liver cancer at enrollment compared to those with HIV coinfection, a finding which has been described in other studies. 

We observed a significant difference between the two groups in the prevalence of CD4 cell counts < 100 cells/µL at enrollment (9% in HBV mono vs. 21% in HIV coinfected, p = 0.02). This finding is consistent with prior studies which demonstrate that HIV progression may be delayed in the setting of HBV coinfection [31–33], suggesting that cellular immune response in HBV monoinfected individuals may be superior to that in those with coinfection. However, we also demonstrate that plasma HIV RNA levels were significantly higher in those with HBV monoinfection (median 3,270 copies/mL) compared to HIV coinfection (median 95 copies/mL, p = 0.01), a finding which suggests that viral suppression was more frequent in the coinfected group which could be explained by superior use of antiretroviral therapy in the HIV coinfected group. These observations suggest that the HIV pathogenesis may be different in those with HBV/HIV coinfection compared to those with HBV monoinfection. These data also suggest that individuals with HBV monoinfection may be more infectious than those with HIV coinfection, as they will have higher levels of plasma HIV RNA, which is correlated with HIV-1 infectiousness [34]. Thus, the HIV treatment program in resource-limited settings may need to prioritize HIV-infected individuals with HBV coinfection for earlier initiation of antiretroviral therapy to achieve higher rates of viral suppression and reduce HIV-1 transmission. The researchers from the University of California San Diego School of Medicine and Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) used a mouse model of HBV infection and co-infection with HIV to examine the impact of HBV on HIV-1 replication, virus-host interactions and disease progression in the absence and presence of antiretroviral therapy (ART). The study results are published in the February 1, 2023, online edition of the journal Nature Microbiology.

“HIV-1 and HBV are co-pandemic worldwide, and co-infection with both viruses in humans is frequent,” said first author Tae-Young Kang, PhD, instructor in the Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Medicine, UC San Diego. “The liver is the main target for both HBV and HIV-1, leading to significant morbidity and mortality from both chronic HBV and HIV-1 infections. Despite their clinical overlap, the interaction between HBV and HIV-1, and its impact on disease progression and treatment, are poorly understood.”

The researchers sought to better understand the impact of HBV on disease progression in an HIV-1-infected host and during antiretroviral therapy. To do this, they used a mouse model to simulate HBV and HIV-1 infection in humans. The mice were bred to express human liver cell receptors for HBV and HIV-1 in their livers, and the researchers co-infected these mice with HBV and a strain of HIV-1 specific to humans (clade M).

The researchers then examined the levels of HIV-1 in the blood and livers of the mice and compared these to levels of HBV and the extent of liver injury and inflammation. They found that the presence of HBV slowed the replication and reduced the levels of HIV-1 in the blood and liver of the mice. This was true for mice treated with ART and those that were not.

According to the researchers, these findings suggest that HBV curbs HIV-1 replication through a hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg)-dependent mechanism that is independent of ART. They also found that HBV infection led to the preferential recruitment of CD8+ T cells into the liver and a shift in the CD4+ T helper cell response away from Th2 and toward a Th1 response.

The study, published online July 15 in the journal Scientific Reports, is the first to characterize the molecular mechanisms by which curcumin treats SARS-CoV-2 infection in the lungs of infected mice. The researchers, led by Zhao-Yong Sun, Ph.D., of the University of Wyoming, found that curcumin blocks the replication of the virus in the lungs by targeting the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro) and the papain-like protease (PLpro), large viral enzymes that the virus needs to replicate. The enzymes are important because they help the virus to evade the immune system and also to evade the drugs that are used to treat the infection.

In the first study, 34 patients with HBV only were randomly assigned to either 12 weeks of lamivudine or to 48 weeks of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) plus emtricitabine (FTC). In the second study, 43 patients with both HBV and HIV were randomly assigned to either 48 weeks of TDF plus FTC or to 48 weeks of TDF plus FTC plus tenofovir alafenamide (TAF). After 48 weeks of therapy, patients in the first study who received TDF plus FTC had significantly greater decreases in HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) levels compared with those who received lamivudine (a decrease from a mean baseline of 6.63 to 1.69 copies/mL versus a decrease from 6.71 to 3.05 copies/mL; P = 0.01). After 48 weeks of therapy, patients in the second study who received TDF plus FTC plus TAF had significantly greater decreases in HBsAg levels compared with those who received TDF plus FTC (a decrease from a mean baseline of 7.58 to 1.93 copies/mL versus a decrease from 7.61 to 3.04 copies/mL; P = 0.01). The authors concluded that HIV/HBV coinfected patients who start HIV treatment with TDF plus FTC plus TAF have greater HBV suppression than those who start treatment with TDF plus FTC alone.

This research was published in Annals of Internal Medicine on Annals.org.

samples.hyp: The overall aim of this study was to investigate if young women who were pregnant or had given birth within the past year had an increased risk of developing a severe course of COVID-19 when compared to young women who had never been pregnant. The secondary aim was to investigate whether there are any differences in clinical characteristics and symptoms between the different groups of young women. We included women aged 16-45 years in the Nordic countries, the United Kingdom, the United States and Brazil. A total of 236 young women were included in this study. Of these, 82 women had given birth in the past year or were currently pregnant. The results showed that young women who were pregnant or had given birth within a year had a higher risk of developing a severe course of COVID-19 when compared to young women who had never been pregnant, even after adjustment for potential confounders. We assessed the following possible confounders: age, smoking, comorbidities, time of symptom onset in relation to time of pregnancy onset. All information used in the analysis was collected by a questionnaire sent to all participants. The questionnaire was not designed to exclude or preferentially include women with a certain pregnancy status, and all women were asked to fill it out, regardless of pregnancy status. The high response rate among both groups supports that the results are likely to be applicable to a similar group of women in the general population. It is biologically plausible that the risk of a severe COVID-19 disease is increased during pregnancy since pregnant women undergo various hormonal changes and immunological adaptations during gestation. These adaptations may increase the risk of developing a severe form of COVID-19, as this disease is caused by a virus that enters the body through the respiratory system and may activate the same hormonal and immunological systems that are affected by pregnancy. Pregnant women have been reported to experience a delay in symptoms onset when compared to non-pregnant women. This might indicate a different immune response, but further investigation is needed to clarify if this is related to pregnancy or to other factors that young pregnant women are exposed to, such as the man with whom they conceived the pregnancy. This research work is an assessment of the impact of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger state. The research work aims to assess the impact of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in the area and to identify the challenges women are facing in their day-to-day running of their businesses. More women are starting businesses in Niger, but they need more security to grow the economy, a new report says.
The number of women setting up businesses in Niger has increased in the last few years, according to a report by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

But the report says they still face a number of challenges, including lack of access to finance and limited opportunities to get training and develop their skills.

The report says that if these challenges are addressed, it could help the country achieve its goal of becoming an upper-middle-income economy by 2030.

The report was presented to IMF officials on Wednesday, who are in the West African country for a two-week visit.

The IMF said in a statement that it was important for the government to create an environment that was conducive for business, and that this would help to reduce poverty and boost economic growth.

It said that by increasing the number of women in the labour force, it would help to close the gender gap and increase productivity.

The IMF said it looked forward to continuing to work with Niger on economic reform and to support the country's development plans.

This is a major public health problem, as preterm births are the leading cause of newborn deaths and other short-term complications among newborns. There are many reasons why a woman may deliver before 37 weeks, and researchers are still trying to understand all of them. However, a new study has found that preterm births are more common among women who have experienced certain stressors, such as intimate partner violence (IPV), and among women who have had certain infections during pregnancy. The study was conducted in Washington state, and it included 345 women who had preterm births and 1,006 women who had full-term births. The women who had preterm births were more likely to report experiencing IPV and to have had a bacterial infection during their pregnancy. The type of bacterial infection that was most commonly seen among the women who had preterm births was an infection with the bacteria Streptococcus, which can cause symptoms such as fever, chills, and vaginal discharge. The results of this study suggest that IPV and infection with Streptococcus may be risk factors for preterm birth. However, it is important to note that this is an observational study, which means that it cannot prove that IPV or infection with Streptococcus causes preterm birth. More research is needed to confirm these findings and to better understand the relationship between stress, infection, and preterm birth. In the meantime, it is important for women who are pregnant or who are trying to get pregnant to take care of their health and to seek medical care if they experience any health problems or if they are exposed to stressors such as IPV.

We hypothesized that high concentrations of iron, zinc, and copper in the maternal plasma may induce preterm birth by increasing the release of proinflammatory cytokines.


The objective of this study was to evaluate the association between high concentrations of micronutrients in the maternal plasma and preterm delivery.


We conducted a case–control study using plasma samples from 65 women who delivered at <37 weeks of gestation (cases) and 65 controls matched for maternal age, ethnicity, gestational age, and week of delivery. Concentrations of iron, zinc, and copper were measured in the plasma samples by atomic absorption spectrophotometry.


The plasma iron, zinc, and copper concentrations were significantly higher in the cases than in the controls (175.4 ± 64.5 vs 142.1 ± 47.1 μg/dL, P = 0.003; 1.12 ± 0.16 vs 1.01 ± 0.10 μg/dL, P = 0.01; and 112.8 ± 31.8 vs 99.6 ± 27.4 μg/dL, P = 0.02, respectively). The iron concentration was a strong predictor of preterm delivery, with an area under the curve of 0.89 (95% confidence interval 0.75–1.00; P = 0.03). There was a trend toward an association between preterm delivery and high maternal plasma copper concentration; this association was strong when the cases were stratified into those who delivered at <34 weeks of gestation (n = 28) and those who delivered at 34–36 weeks of gestation (n = 37). After adjusting for maternal plasma iron and zinc concentrations, the odds ratio (OR) for preterm delivery in the highest versus lowest copper quartile was 5.17 (95% confidence interval 1.41–19.06).


Our results suggest that high concentrations of iron, zinc, and copper in the maternal plasma may induce the release of proinflammatory cytokines, which could lead to preterm birth.

The samples were tested for Zika and other infections, and the women were interviewed about their exposure to mosquitoes and their health during pregnancy.

The researchers found that 32 of the women, or 18 percent, tested positive for Zika virus. The virus causes a illness with fever, rash, joint pain, and red eyes. Most people who become infected never develop symptoms.

The researchers also found that 10 percent of the women had high levels of a Zika virus protein called NS1 in their blood. This indicates a recent Zika infection.

The women with recent or current Zika infections were more likely to have given birth to stillborn babies or to have babies who died soon after birth. They were also more likely to have babies with microcephaly or other brain defects; 7 percent of the babies had microcephaly, and 18 percent had other brain defects.

The researchers also found that 10 percent of the women tested positive for syphilis, 6 percent tested positive for hepatitis B, and 1 percent tested positive for hepatitis C.

Malawi has a history of outbreaks of Zika and other mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue virus and chikungunya virus. “These findings will be used to improve our surveillance system and to strengthen our prevention and control activities against Zika and other mosquito-borne diseases in Malawi,” says Dr. Alex Ndhlovu, medical officer for malaria at the Malawi Ministry of Health.

Zika virus is spread by the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito. These mosquitoes are found in over 100 countries in the Americas, Africa, Europe, and Asia. Travel-related cases have also been reported in the Pacific Islands and India. Most infections in Africa have occurred because infected people traveled to the continent from other countries. There have been a few cases of Zika virus transmission in Africa that did not involve travel. But the researchers say it is not clear if these cases indicate ongoing, local transmission of the virus in Africa.

The World Health Organization declared the Zika virus outbreak a public health emergency in February 2016. The outbreak in the Americas continues, with Uruguay reporting its first case of locally acquired Zika infection in November 2017. Because the virus can cause birth defects, the outbreak has led many countries and territories to recommend that women avoid pregnancy or delay becoming pregnant while the outbreak continues.

Dr. Lynne Howden-Curtis, the lead researcher on the study, said: “Our study adds to the body of evidence suggesting a protective effect of selenium against pancreatic cancer. While selenium is a vital nutrient for the human body, with the body only needing about 55 mg of selenium per day, it is not something that is produced by the human body itself, meaning that it needs to be obtained from food or supplements. Selenium can be found in a variety of foods, with examples including nuts, grains, and organ meats. However, it is not something that is found in very high levels within food, so many people choose to take selenium supplements to ensure that they are getting enough of the nutrient. At what level should people take selenium supplements? The answer to that question may not be what you think.

samples.ref: Ìwà Ìtọpasẹ̀-ilé, Ìṣòótọ́ sí Ààyè àti Ìjẹgàba-ààyè Ìjàpá abígbá-pẹrẹsẹ (Malacochersus tornieri) ní Kenya

The Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) is a critically endangered tortoise endemic to Kenya and Somalia. There is increasing interest in ex situ and in situ conservation of this species due to its small population size, ongoing habitat destruction and trade. Radio telemetry was used to study homing ability and territoriality of this species at Lake Nakuru National Park, Kenya. Six individuals were released at sites away from their home range and monitored for 17 days. Four of the individuals (66%) homed back to their home range. The failure of two individuals to home back may be due to the fact that they were translocated a further distance from their home range (1,200m and 500m) than the other individuals (100m and 200m). During the 17 days that the tortoises were released, there was overlap in the use of space particularly during the day. At the end of the 17 days, the tortoises were recaptured and it was found that the males had maintained their home ranges while the female’s home range had expanded. Towards the end of the study, the males became aggressive towards each other when encountered within their home ranges. This suggests that the males had marked their home ranges and may have defended them. The fact that the female expanded her home range at the end of the study suggests that she was either advertising her home range or defending it. In order to conserve this species, ex situ and in situ conservation should be carried out in conjunction with each other. Conservation measures such as building fences around the home ranges of this species in order to prevent translocation of individuals and trade should be carried out.

Here we use 19 years of data on space use by Steller sea lions (Eumetopias jubatus) at three colonies in Alaska to examine individual variation in site fidelity, colony fidelity and maternally based site fidelity and the influence of these patterns on population-level indicators. We found that all three colony sites had a relatively high proportion of resident animals (34-40%) that returned to the same location each year. However, there was variation in the degree of site fidelity by colony, with animals at Amlukna Colony the most likely to return to the same location (81% within 100 m and 93% within 300 m), followed by the Western Brooks Falls population (57% and 76%, respectively) and the Eastern Brooks Falls population with the lowest levels of site fidelity (22% and 36%). We also found that 70% of females at the Brooks Falls populations returned to the location where they had raised their young the previous year, and of those, 90% returned to the same location. These females showed high site fidelity to both the general area where they had raised their young (i.e., the Brooks Falls colony) and to specific locations within that area where they had hauled out in previous years. Female site fidelity was a better predictor of population-level indicators at the Brooks Falls colonies (R2 = 0.37 and 0.65) than was colony-level site fidelity (R2 = 0.11 and 0.23), particularly for indicators sensitive to local levels of predation or food availability. Our results indicate that conservation and management decisions may benefit from accounting for such individual-level patterns of space use.

Pancake tortoises are masterful navigators. (Image: Alex Bond)

Pancake tortoises are masterful navigators, able to travel up to 30 times their own body length in a single trip. But one group of lost tortoises went off-course – and scientists have discovered why.

In 2017, conservationists in Madagascar were concerned when a group of 118 pancake tortoises failed to return to their feeding grounds after a flood. The animals were nowhere to be seen, and the team feared the worst.

Now, years later, scientists have traced the animals to a site 13 kilometres (8 miles) away. It seems the animals were lured off-course by the scent of decaying vegetation.

“We were relieved to find them safe,” says lead study author Alex Bond of the University of Exeter in the UK. “But we were also very interested to find that they had moved to a site driven by the availability of food, rather than a homing instinct.”

Pancake tortoises are the only tortoise species known to be able to orientate over long distances using the position of key feeding sites in relation to the sun, stars and mountains. The new findings suggest that this ability is more limited than previously thought.

The team used DNA from droppings to identify the animals and track their movements. They found that the group had moved to a site with a different elevation to their home feeding grounds, which would have changed the angle of the sun and key stars.

The scientists also found that the animals had moved to a site with more available food, which could have been the driving force behind their decision to move.

Pancake tortoises are listed as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. The IUCN estimates that the total population has declined by more than 80 per cent in the last 30 years, with the species facing threats from habitat loss, hunting and the pet trade.

Journal reference: Journal of Animal Ecology, DOI: 10.1111/1365-2656.13379

The study, led by the University of Turku, Finland, was published in the journal Animal Cognition.

The East African pancake tortoise is a rare species that lives in arid areas of East Africa. The shell of the turtle is not dome-shaped like that of most other tortoises, but rather resembles a pancake, which is how it got its name. The species was thought to be extinct until 1890, when one of the animals was found in a Zanzibar herbarium. Since then, no one has seen the species in the wild except for one group found in northern Kenya in 2010. The tortoises are under threat from collectors, who capture the animals for trade. The species is also threatened by climate change, as rising temperatures have reduced the amount of food available to the animals.

The researchers wanted to study how the tortoises find their way back to their burrows after being moved to a new location. The scientists, including PhD student Juha Vesterinen from the University of Turku, marked the animals with GPS loggers and moved them to a new location 1.4 km away from their home. The loggers stopped working when the batteries ran out, but the scientists had placed the loggers so that they would fall off the shell when the batteries died, and they found the loggers near the tortoises’ original burrows. The researchers also moved four of the animals over a longer distance of 6.5 km but were surprised when all four of the tortoises were found back at their original burrows after two weeks. The researchers think the tortoises may have been guided home by the Earth’s magnetic field, as other tortoise species are thought to do. However, more research is needed to confirm this hypothesis.

The researchers decided to use the Hermann’s tortoise as a model species to investigate how it uses visual cues to find its way home.

The researchers constructed a circular outdoor arena with a central “home” platform and surrounded this on all sides by a metal fence to prevent escape routes. They then released 14 tortoises into the arena and marked their homing success by the amount of time they spent on the home platform. The amount of time spent on the home platform by chance alone is 20 seconds, as there is no visual difference between the home platform and the surrounding arena floor. The researchers found that four of the tortoises spent significantly more time on the home platform than 20 seconds (average 76, 53, 29 and 24 minutes). They also found that the tortoises showed a preference for the right of centre, even when the home platform was positioned to the left of centre. The time these tortoises spent on the right of the home platform was significantly greater than 20 seconds (average 152, 239, 172 and 204 minutes). Interestingly, two of the successful homing tortoises also showed a preference for a specific spot on the right of the home platform.

The results of this study suggest that Hermann’s tortoises may use a combination of two navigational techniques to home: 1) using celestial polarised light to navigate in a straight path towards the equator and 2) using visual landmarks on the equator to get back to their home burrow. The researchers plan to continue their study to investigate these possibilities.

At the time, the researchers had been using radio collars to track the animals’ movements, and they noticed that the animals were all heading to a specific area, which was about 30 kilometres away. 

‘We decided to try to move them to a new location, about 100 kilometres away, and see if they would come back home,’ Dr Kays said. 

The team spent a week catching and relocating the animals, using pitfall traps – which are pits filled with water laced with fish sex attractants. 

‘The animals are attracted to the traps by the bait, then we carefully scoop them into containers so we can weigh them, take biological samples like skin and hair, and fit them with a radio collar before we release them back into the wild,’ Dr Kays said. 

The team caught and released 21 brown tree snakes, and were surprised to find that 13 of them – 62 per cent – had returned to their original capture site. 

‘We were expecting, if they were moving in response to some kind of cue, that they would come back to their original home,’ Dr Kays said. 

‘But 62 per cent returning to the original home is a much stronger response than we were expecting.’

samples.hyp:
This is likely to be due to the fact that the landscape in which they live is so patchy, with food resources and suitable shelter being intermittent. Living in the same area also minimises the risks of predation or having to cross areas that might be dangerous to them.
We know very little about how these animals live in the wild, so understanding more about their natural behaviour is very important if we are to ensure their long-term survival.
The researchers used GPS devices to track the movements of ten tortoises in the Makira Island, Malawi. They found that the animals always returned to the same general area after moving away to forage, even if this involved travelling several hundred metres. The animals also showed a strong preference for resting in the same burrow, and would only use a different one if the original was no longer habitable (e.g. if it had been flooded or collapsed).
When the researchers played the recorded sounds of a male and female tortoises together, to imitate courtship calls, the males moved towards the source of the sound. The males travel long distances to find a mate, and this could have important implications for their survival. If the landscape is such that the tortoises are unable to find a mate, their chances of successful breeding are reduced and their population could decline as a result.
The researchers say that their findings will help to inform conservation plans for the species, and highlight the importance of maintaining large areas of intact habitat in order to ensure the long-term survival of tortoise populations.
The pancake tortoise is listed as Endangered in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, and is thought to have declined by 80% in the last 30 years. It is primarily threatened by habitat loss, but over-exploitation for the international wildlife trade is also a major threat.
This work was funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, the Natural Environment Research Council, the University of Sheffield, the Turtle Conservation Trust and the Mwaza Conservation and Community Project.

Dr. Auliya said: “We were really lucky to find these animals. They are very cryptic and found in a highly threatened habitat. 

“Also, the population is still big enough to withstand some loss of individuals, but the main reason for the stable population size is rather the high natality of the species. 

“Human impact on the habitat is a major issue, and the turtles are frequently killed by cars when crossing the road. 

“Another major issue is livestock grazing, which often affects the turtles when they come out of the water to feed on grass.”


Dr. Auliya and colleagues now want to set up a long-term monitoring program in collaboration with local people, to catch the animals and mark them with tags to find out how often they leave the beach and how far they go into the desert. 

“We also want to fit satellite transmitters to some of them to track their movements overseas.” 

Co-author Dr. Anders P. Berg said: “This is the first time that we have been able to identify individuals that return to their natal beach to nest, which is crucial from a conservation point of view. 

“We believe that this is due to some unknown homing mechanism, and not simply due to random movements or failures to exit the area where they hatched. 

“Only a few animal species on Earth have been shown to use such mechanisms to return to their birthplace, and none of the 350+ turtle species has been shown to do this. 

“This makes the desert tortoises all the more interesting, and we hope our results will motivate others to study this even further.”


Lead author Dr. Ilaria Dall’Olio, from the University of Bologna, said: “Understanding how animals return to their natal sites is one of the major questions in ecology.

“These findings are a fundamental step for the conservation of this species and our results highlight the importance of protecting all known nesting areas, as some of them may have high returns of individuals each year.

“This will ensure that there is a constant supply of individuals for future nesting events, which is a key factor for the recovery of the species.”

This is a randomized controlled trial of a 15-week social communication intervention for young children with autism in Uganda. The intervention, which is designed for community providers, aims to teach children with autism and their non-autistic peers to make friends and engage in back-and-forth conversation. The intervention consists of (1) 12 weeks of twice-weekly group therapy sessions and (2) 3 weeks of maintenance home visits. The primary outcome will be change in children’s social communication abilities. Secondary outcomes include change in child and parent stress, and child daily living skills. The study will also generate evidence on the feasibility and acceptability of the intervention in Uganda. This study will be the first randomized controlled trial of a social communication intervention for children with autism in Africa, and the first study of this intervention in a low-resource setting.

Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder that is characterized by social withdrawal, communication difficulties, and restricted and repetitive behaviors. A growing number of children across the globe are being diagnosed with autism, and the condition is increasingly being identified in low-resource and middle-income countries. In Uganda, the prevalence of autism has been estimated at approximately 1 in 54 children (Bakken & Tager-Flusberg, 2021). There has been a rapid increase in the number of children being diagnosed with autism in Uganda, but there are significant barriers to effective treatment. For example, there are no standardized services for young children with autism in the country, and there are fewer than 5 evidence-based autism interventions that have been developed and tested in low-resource contexts. There are also considerable cultural sensitivities to many evidence-based autism interventions that have been developed in Western countries, and it is important to develop interventions that address the needs of families and communities in low-resource countries.

This project builds on our ongoing work developing a family-based social communication intervention for young children with autism in the United States. We investigated if lower doses given by intramuscular route could achieve serum concentrations similar to those achieved by intravenous therapy.

We performed a prospective, open-label, non-inferiority, randomised controlled trial in two South African sites with a 2:1 ratio and central randomisation. We included children aged 6 months to 16 years with culture-confirmed tuberculous meningitis. All patients received standardised medical and surgical treatment. In the intravenous rifampicin group patients received 10 mg/kg twice daily while in the intramuscular group they received 5 mg/kg once daily. Both groups also received 10 mg/kg bodyweight rifampicin and 10 mg/kg bodyweight pyrazinamide intramuscularly once daily, and 500 mg/ kg bodyweight ethambutol orally twice daily, and 40 mg/kg bodyweight isoniazid orally once daily. The primary outcome was cure rate at 2 months, based on a modification of the World Health Organization standard scheme, and assessed by intention to treat.

30 patients were enrolled, 15 in each group. The groups were well balanced for age, sex, and disease severity. The cure rate in the intravenous group was 73% compared with 40% in the intramuscular group, a between-group difference of 33% (95% CI 0·0 to 58·7; difference in proportions −0·27, 0·0 to 0·48; p=·049). There was no significant difference in adverse events between the groups.

Our study shows that intramuscular rifampicin at a daily dose of 5 mg/kg bodyweight generates rifampicin concentrations within the accepted therapeutic range. The lower cure rate in the intramuscular group might be due to poor tolerability and/or compliance, which makes a case for controlled introduction of intramuscular rifampicin in tuberculous meningitis.

High dose pills can be tested on HIV patients with TB meningitis

A new trial will test a treatment that combines anti-HIV and anti-TB drugs for people with HIV and drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) and who have TB meningitis, a severe form of TB infection that affects the brain and spinal cord.

The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), part of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), launched the first site of this study in Botswana. The HIV Vaccine Trials Network (HVTN), which is based at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center in Seattle, Washington, and the AIDS Clinical Trials Group (ACTG), based at the University of California, San Francisco, are collaborating on the trial, which will enroll participants at sites in Botswana, South Africa, Lesotho, USA and Switzerland. For more information about this study, please visit http://clinicaltrials.gov/ict/ and search for study NCT01274220 or contact the study sites directly.

We are looking for healthy people who:
  • are between the ages of 18 and 65
  • test positive for being HIV-negative
  • agree to try to become HIV-infected through an experimental exposure
  • have not taken TB medications in the last 8 weeks
  • have a high likelihood of being exposed to HIV through sex, injecting drugs, or other risk behavior
  • test positive for being susceptible to TB disease
  • agree to take study pills daily for 48 weeks
  • agree to undergo periodic physical exams and lab tests
  • agree to have a lumbar puncture (also called a spinal tap)
  • agree to use condoms and practice safer sex 100% of the time during the 48 weeks
  • agree not to become pregnant by using two forms of birth control simultaneously for 48 weeks
  • agree to have participated in the study for 3 months after taking the last study pill.

For more information, please contact:

Botswana: 267-392-7479

United States: 206-667-6207

The drug is already being tested in a large trial in Cape Town.

The results of the small trial were published in the New England Journal of Medicine. The trial was led by Frank van der Westhuizen at the University of KwaZulu-Natal and Gandhi Ningaluka at Médecins Sans Frontières.

The trial involved 71 HIV-positive patients with tuberculosis meningitis. They were randomly assigned to receive either rifampicin or standard treatment. The drug was given as a high dose for the first two weeks and then a standard dose for the rest of the treatment.

The 34 patients who received high- dose rifampicin for the first two weeks fared much better than the 37 patients who received standard treatment. The patients on high-dose rifampicin were more likely to survive and their mental function was better preserved.

The difference in outcomes was most striking in patients who were very sick at the start of treatment. Of these patients 18% died while receiving high-dose rifampicin compared to 59% of those who received standard treatment.

It is still too early to tell whether rifampicin can improve patient outcomes. The main trial which is being done in Cape Town can provide a definitive answer to this question. This trial is large enough to show whether rifampicin helps with patient outcomes, but not large enough to show small differences.

The researchers will present their findings at the Conference for Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in Seattle next month.

Source: ScienceDaily

The Centre is also a co-focal point of the World Health Organisation’s Global Meningitis Control Initiative.

The SA-TRIM consortium comprises the Desmond Tutu TB Centre at SU, the University of Cape Town, the South African Medical Research Council, the South African National Tuberculosis Programme, the University of KwaZulu-Natal, the University of Bremen in Germany and the University of Cambridge in the UK. English: The prevalence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is increasing globally and is expected to continue to do so, especially in low- and middle-income countries. COPD is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. A large proportion of patients are in low- and middle-income countries, which are often also experiencing high burdens of co-morbidities and limited health-care resources. The majority of COPD-related deaths are estimated to occur after discharge from hospital, but post-discharge follow-up care is often inadequate. Telehealth interventions have been investigated as a way of improving patient outcomes after hospital discharge, but most studies have been conducted in high-income countries with the exception of one study conducted in South Africa. This study investigated the use of a multi-modal telehealth system for monitoring patients with COPD after hospital discharge. The system integrated the use of a smart device, activity tracker, and a gas analyzer that can be used to monitor key COPD outcomes such as lung function and activity levels. The study aimed to determine the feasibility of the system in terms of patient’s and caregiver’s acceptance, safety, and the ability of the system to capture the required data (i.e. feasibility of use).

Criteria for exclusion were: too ill to be discharged, patient unwilling to participate, and inability to perform spirometry. “This study highlights the need to develop new drugs for the treatment of TB meningitis that are effective and safe to use in the brain. 

“Rifampicin is an essential drug for the treatment of TB and we need to ensure that any new drugs developed for TB also work against TB meningitis.”

Dr Tanya Warner, Research Fellow at the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre, Imperial College London, added: 

“We already know that TB meningitis is harder to treat than other forms of TB and that alternative drugs are needed. Now we have a better understanding of why some of the current treatments for TB may not be as effective when treating meningitis.

Dr Ajit Lalvani, Director of the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre Clinical Research Facility, Imperial College London, said: 

“Tuberculous meningitis is a medical emergency and the most severe and deadly form of TB. We already use rifampicin to treat TB but it does not cross the blood-brain barrier. Our study shows that rifampicin is taken up by the cells of the brain in a different way to other parts of the body, which may explain why it is less effective against TB meningitis. However, the finding also suggests how to target the drug directly into the brain to enhance its effectiveness against TB meningitis.”

A laboratory incubation study

The overall objective of this study was to investigate the effects of combined compost and biochar application on soil quality and plant growth. A highly weathered coastal savanna soil (Aerenosol) was incubated at 25 degrees C and 60% M.S.E for two months under undisturbed (control), composted cowpeat (CP) at 0.1 and 0.2% v/v, biochar (BC) at 0.1 and 0.2% v/v, and combined composted cowpeat and biochar (CP+BC) at 0.1 and 0.2% v/v. Soil respiration, soil respiration quotient (SRQ), soil microbial biomass content (SMB), available phosphorus (AvP), potassium (AvK), and electrical conductivity (EC) were measured. Greater values of soil respiration, SMB, AvP, AvK, and EC were observed in composted cowpeat treated soil, while the highest values were observed in the combined composted cowpeat and biochar treated soil. The highest plant growth (height and dry biomass) was also observed in the combined composted cowpeat and biochar treated soil. The results from this study showed that combined composted cowpeat and biochar application improved the quality of the Aerenosol, and thus, this combined material can be used as a soil amendment for improving coastal savanna soils.

However, the effect of combined application of biochar and compost has not been studied yet. Therefore, the objective of this study was to investigate the effect of a combination of biochar and compost on soil properties and on the growth of okra, pepper, and tomato. A field experiment was conducted in the 2017/2018 growing season at the research area of the Institute of Agricultural Sciences, Swiss Federal Research Institute for Agricultural Research, Zurich, Switzerland. The experimental design was a randomized block design with a factorial arrangement of treatments. Factors were three rates of biochar (0, 6.25, and 12.5 t/ha) and two levels of compost application (with and without compost). Compost was applied at a rate of 25 t/ha. The results showed that the combined application of biochar and compost improved soil properties, such as soil bulk density, soil water content, available water holding capacity, and available nutrients (N, P, K, Mg, and Ca). The application of biochar and compost increased the number of fruits per plant, fruit weight, and marketable yield of okra, pepper, and tomato. The highest marketable yields of okra (23.1 t/ha), pepper (29.7 t/ha), and tomato (57.7 t/ha) were obtained with the combined application of biochar (12.5 t/ha) and compost. According to the Pearson correlation and regression analysis, the marketable yields of okra, pepper, and tomato increased with an increase in the rate of biochar, soil water content, available water holding capacity, and available nutrients (N, P, K, Mg, and Ca). The interaction effect of biochar and compost on the marketable yield of the tested crops was significant. The combined application of biochar and compost can be recommended to improve soil properties and to increase the marketable yield of vegetable crops.

The experiment was set up as a completely randomized design with three replicates. The treatments were: control (unamended soil); soil amended with biochar types at the specified rates; soil amended with 1 % w/w inorganic fertilizer (NPK 20-10-10) and soil amended with 1 % w/w inorganic fertilizer plus biochar types at the specified rates. The experimental units were installed in the greenhouse of the University of Rova Andrianavalona in Fianarantsoa, Madagascar, and watered daily to maintain 60 % field capacity. After 30 days of incubation, the soil moisture, pH, electrical conductivity, organic carbon (OC), nitrate (NO3 - ), available phosphorus (P), potassium (K), enargite (FeO), heme (Fe), total nitrogen (N), and ammonium (NH4 + ) of each treatment were measured. The results showed that the amendment of acrisol with biochar types and inorganic fertilizer increased the soil pH, OC, EC, P, K, enargite, heme, N, and NH4 + . The application of biochar types alone or with inorganic fertilizer increased soil moisture. The highest values of soil pH, OC, EC, P, K, enargite, heme, N, and NH4 + were observed in the treatments with compost, rcocomp, and cococomp, respectively. The highest values of soil moisture were observed in the treatments with compost, rbio, cco300, and cco700, respectively. The application of biochar types with inorganic fertilizer increased the content of OC, P, K, enargite, heme, N, and NH4 + , and decreased the content of NO3 - . The highest content of OC, P, K, enargite, heme, N, and NH4 + were observed in the treatments with rcocomp and cococomp, respectively. The highest content of NO3 - was observed in the treatment with inorganic fertilizer. The application of biochar types with inorganic fertilizer increased the ratio of C/N, and decreased the ratio of NO3 - /NH4 + . The highest ratio of C/N was observed in the treatment with cco300, whereas the lowest ratio of NO3 - /NH4 + was observed in the treatment with inorganic fertilizer.

English text:
Biochar and compost improve soil quality for crops
Posted by: Eliseo Dario | on April 9, 2015

Eliseo Dario
You can read the original post here:

Soil quality affects crop growth and yield in a variety of ways. It’s important to have good soil quality to produce quality crops. Researchers continue to study the effects of biochar and compost on soil quality. They have found that adding these to soil can have a positive effect on crop growth and yield.

Researchers at the University of Florida found that maize yield was increased by 208% when biochar and compost were added to soil. They also found that the amount of water a soil holds, known as available water capacity, was increased by 32%. This is important because it allows the soil to hold more water and therefore reduces the need for additional watering of the crop. The amount of water a soil holds is also affected by the amount of sand or clay in the soil. The more sand or clay in the soil, the less water the soil holds.

Biochar and compost can also help reduce the amount of nitrogen leached from a soil. Nitrogen is a nutrient that is essential for plant growth. Too much or too little nitrogen can be harmful to crops. If a soil has too much nitrogen, the nutrient can leach into the groundwater or be lost through volatilization. Volatilization occurs when elements in the soil, such as nitrogen, are turned into a gas and released into the atmosphere. Researchers found that adding biochar and compost can reduce the amount of nitrogen leached from a soil by 95% and the amount lost through volatilization by 92%.

samples.src: This study investigated how biochar, a highly stable, carbon-rich material made from discarded biomass, can be used to improve the quality of soils in sub-Saharan Africa.
samples.ref: Ìwádìí yìí ṣiṣẹ́ lóríi bí èédú, tí a ṣẹ̀dá látara báómaàsì, lè di lílò fún ìfikún ìdára ilẹ̀ ní àwọn agbègbe gúsù ilẹ̀ Áfíríkà.
samples.hyp:
Biochar is known to have a high surface area, which allows it to hold onto nutrients and water, and also to act as a slow-release fertilizer. We conducted a series of laboratory incubation experiments to assess changes in soil properties, and the potential of biochar to improve soil quality, as well as crop growth and yield. We also did a systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate the effectiveness of biochar in improving crop yield, and to identify where further research is needed.

The laboratory incubation experiments showed that the addition of biochar to soil increased potentially mineralizable nitrogen (N), available phosphorus (P), and potassium (K), as well as soil water content and bulk density. Mechanistically, we found that biochar promotes N retention through a combination of physico-chemical and biological processes, and that it stimulates microbial growth and the subsequent release of N and P. We also observed a positive response of wheat (Triticum aestivum) and tea (Camellia sinensis) to biochar treatment, in terms of shoot length and biomass accumulation. The meta-analysis showed that biochar amendment significantly increased crop yield; the response was greater for cereals than for legumes. However, the amount of biochar used in the experiments varied over two orders of magnitude and the form and origin of the biochar also differed. Therefore, more research is needed to assess the response of different crops to biochar amendment, and to identify the minimum application rates and properties of biochar required to improve crop yield.

. This is the underlying principle of the Soil Management Transfer (SMT) project, implemented by the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT), in Kenya and Rwanda. 

The SMT project is one of the CIMMYT-led initiatives implemented under the Comprehensive Africa Agriculture Development Program (CAADP) framework, which is a key strategic investment program of the New Partnership for Africa’s Development (NEPAD) plans. The SMT project is funded by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA) and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

The SMT project aims to increase agricultural productivity and reduce poverty in Africa through improved soil management practices. The project does this by building the capacity of small-scale farmers’ organizations to design, implement, and evaluate soil management interventions.

The SMT framework
The SMT project uses a demand-driven approach to determine the soil management interventions that small-scale farmers in a region want and need. To do this, the project uses a participatory process that brings together different stakeholders to discuss and prioritize different soil management interventions. The project then supports the farmers’ organizations in planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating the selected interventions.

The SMT framework has three main components:

  1. Situational analysis: The project starts by conducting a situational analysis of the region’s small-scale farmers. This involves gathering information on the farmers’ soil management practices, challenges, and priorities. The analysis helps the project team better understand the context in which the farmers work.
  2. Design and planning: Based on the situational analysis, the project team works with the farmers to design and plan the soil management interventions. This involves identifying the most pressing soil management issues, setting goals and objectives, and designing activities to achieve them.
  3. Implementation, monitoring, and evaluation: The third component involves implementing the planned interventions, monitoring their progress, and evaluating their impact. This helps the project team learn what works and what doesn’t, and make adjustments as needed.

The SMT framework is flexible and can be adapted to different contexts and priorities. This allows the project to be relevant and responsive to the needs of small-scale farmers in different regions of Africa.

However, the effects of biochar on soil microbial communities are still not well understood. Here, we investigated the impact of biochar addition on soil bacterial communities in two soils (an agricultural and a forest soil) from semi-arid regions in Israel, using a 164-day field incubation study under ambient conditions. The addition of biochar at any of the studied doses (2.5, 5, and 10% by volume) increased soil pH, water holding capacity, and carbon content in both studied soils. Original soil total microbial counts and respiration rates were not significantly affected by the addition of biochar. However, biochar addition shaped the structure of bacterial communities in both studied soils. The addition of biochar resulted in a decrease in the Shannon diversity index, particularly in the forest soil. The structure of bacterial communities was related to changes in soil carbon and pH, as well as to the addition of biochar. The addition of 5% biochar resulted in the highest relative abundance of Firmicutes in both studied soils and the relative abundance of Bacteroidetes predominance in the agricultural soil. The addition of biochar supported the enrichment of particular bacterial groups, such as Cytophaga–Flavobacterium, Intrasporangium, and Variovorax, which are known to assist in carbon and nutrient cycling. Our findings suggest that the addition of biochar can support the establishment of specific bacterial communities, which could be used to design novel, environment-friendly soil amendments for agricultural purposes.
