Biochar without compost was the most effective at increasing soil respiration, and the application of 7.5 t ha−1 of biochar without compost resulted in the highest increase (31%). A new study has shown that biochar from coconut husks can reduce soil-borne pathogens in banana crops and increase crop productivity.

The study titled “Biochar from coconut husk reduces soil-borne pathogens and improves banana growth and yield in Uganda” was conducted by Joseph M. Mwaniki, William R. Mburu, Gaspard W. Kanyarwanda, Yvonne N. Wairimu, Naftali Kiunsi, and Kenneth N. Jarvis at the Department of Forest, Wildlife and Development Studies at Makerere University in Uganda.

The paper was recently published in the journal “Agronomy for Sustainable Development.”

According to the researchers, banana is an important food and income crop for millions of smallholder farmers in East Africa, but productivity is reduced due to soil-borne pathogens and intensive farming practices.

They stated that the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides is limited due to their cost and potential environmental and health risks.

Biochar was identified as a sustainable means to improve soil health and crop productivity.

However, the effectiveness of biochar made from slow-pyrolized coconut husk (PH) in reducing soil-borne pathogens and improving banana growth and yield has not been evaluated.

Therefore, the objective of the study was to evaluate the effect of slow-pyrolized PH biochar on soil-borne pathogens and banana growth and yield under field conditions in Uganda.

The researchers conducted an 8-month field trial from July 2017 to February 2018 in Tororo, Uganda. They applied 20 t ha−1 (10 cm depth) of PH biochar to banana plants of the East African highland bananas (Musa spp.) variety ‘FIA 17’ before planting and compared it with other treatments.

The treatments were:

  • Control (no biochar added)
  • PH biochar at 0, 5, 10, and 15 t ha−1
  • A commercial biochar at 5 t ha−1

Soil samples were collected before the application of biochar and at the end of the experiment to determine the soil microbial biomass and activity, and soil-borne pathogens of banana.

Biochar is a carbon-rich solid material produced by the pyrolysis of biomass in the absence of oxygen. Biochar can be used as a soil additive to improve soil quality and fertility, and it can also be used as a carbon sequestration tool. The first objective of this thesis was to investigate the structure of fibrin fibres in the presence of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and to clarify whether the structure of the fibrin fibre network is altered in patients with RA. The second objective was to investigate whether the altered fibrin fibre network has any relation to the coagulation system, inflammation and autoimmunity.

The structure of fibrin fibres was investigated by transmission electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and small-angle X-ray scattering. The results indicated that fibrin fibres in the presence of RA have a more atypical structure than those in healthy individuals. The atypical fibrin fibre network in RA patients was more likely to form large fibres, fibre bundles and fibre aggregates than the network in healthy individuals. The results from small-angle X-ray scattering indicated that the distance between the fibrin fibres was smaller in the presence of RA. This means that the atypical fibrin fibre network in RA is more densely packed than the network in healthy individuals.

The third objective was to investigate the reason behind the atypical structure of the fibrin fibre network. The results indicated that the atypical structure was not caused by genetic mutations, but by an increased activation of the coagulation system. When the coagulation system is activated, it increases the chance that fibrin monomers will form large fibrin fibres, fibre bundles and fibre aggregates. The results indicated that this was the case in patients with RA. The results also showed that the increased activation of the coagulation system in patients with RA was related to autoimmunity and inflammation.

We hypothesized that citrullination increases the activation state of fibrinogen, resulting in enhanced thrombogenicity.

Human plasma was collected from healthy subjects and patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), and from patients with SLE/APS and previous thrombotic events. Fibrinogen citrullination was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Clotting time was assessed by thrombin-based clotting assays and by tissue factor-based clotting assays. Proteins in fibrin clots were labeled with biotin, and the labeled clots were incubated with streptavidin-conjugated PE and analyzed by flow cytometry. Activation of the alternative complement pathway was measured by chromogenic assay.

Citrullinated fibrinogen reduced the clotting time of healthy control plasma by 10% in thrombin-based clotting assays and by 20% in tissue factor-based clotting assays (p < 0.05). The presence of anticitrullinated fibrinogen antibodies correlated with a decrease in clotting time in thrombin-based clotting assays (r = - 0.395, p = 0.03) and trended toward a decrease in clotting time in tissue factor-based clotting assays (r = - 0.304, p = 0.06). Citrullination increased the amount of fibrin(ogen) in the clots by 25% (p < 0.05) and trended toward an increase in the level of biotin labeling (p = 0.06). Clots made from citrullinated fibrinogen showed decreased levels of activated factor VII, but increased levels of activated factor X (p < 0.05). In addition, citrullinated fibrinogen promoted complement activation.

Fibrinogen citrullination increased its thrombotic potential, suggesting that this process contributes to the thrombotic risk in patients with autoimmune diseases.

Our results show that measures of endothelial dysfunction and fibrin clot characteristics were independently associated with both radiographic erosions and ankylosis, after adjustment for confounders. Patients with greater degrees of endothelial dysfunction had increased inflammation (ESR and CRP), coagulation (fibrinogen) and fibrin clot permeability. Inflammation and coagulation, but not endothelial dysfunction, were associated with an increased risk of spinal cord compression in RA. Our results suggest that there is added risk of spinal cord compression in RA patients with high levels of both IL-6 and D-dimer. This study highlights the importance of a multi-system approach to the assessment of comorbidity in RA.

In brief, 40 ml of whole blood were layered over 35 ml of Ficoll-Paque Plus (GE Healthcare, Freiburg, Germany) and centrifuged at 2,000 g for 30 min at room temperature. This is a novel method to assess the coagulation status of the whole blood, by measuring the change in mechanical properties of the coagulating blood over time21. This study used the thromboelastography curve to define two time-dependent indices: the coagulation index (CI), which is measured as the percentage decrease in the oscillation amplitude from the baseline to 10 minutes, and the strength index (SI), which is measured as the percentage increase in the oscillation amplitude from 10 to 60 minutes. The higher the CI, the lower the time to form a fibrin clot, and the higher the SI, the higher the clot strength.

TEG parameters relating to coagulation initiation (R and K), rate of fibrin cross-linking (α-Angle), and time to reach maximum thrombus generation (TMRTG) were attenuated in RA patients. Consistent with these findings, levels of coagulation factors VIII, IX, and XI were reduced in RA patients. In addition, levels of the coagulation inhibitor, antithrombin III were increased in RA patients. TEG-based monitoring of coagulation status in RA patients, identified a specific profile of coagulation defects that could be overcome by fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and/or cryoprecipitate. In patients treated with FFP and cryoprecipitate, TEG parameters returned to the reference range and levels of coagulation factors VIII, IX, XI, and antithrombin III were restored to normal. In a recent pilot study, we have demonstrated the clinical utility of TEG-based coagulation monitoring in two RA patients who underwent orthopedic surgery.2 In both patients, TEG-based coagulation monitoring identified a specific coagulation defect that was successfully overcome by the administration of FFP and/or cryoprecipitate. For example, in one patient, TEG data demonstrated a decrease in factor VIII (FVIII) and an increase in antithrombin III (AT-III), which is consistent with a deficiency state in the intrinsic pathway of coagulation. This patient received 1000 ml of FFP and 1000 units of cryoprecipitate, which resulted in a complete correction of the TEG parameters. In this patient, as well as a second patient who also required administration of FFP and cryoprecipitate, we performed standard laboratory testing for the coagulation factors, which in both cases, demonstrated a decrease in factors VIII, IX, and XI, as well as an increase in AT-III. The administration of FFP and cryoprecipitate in these patients resulted in an increase in the levels of coagulation factors VIII, IX, XI and a reduction in AT-III. This case series demonstrates the clinical utility of TEG-based coagulation monitoring in patients with RA who are undergoing orthopedic surgery. It also highlights the limitations of standard laboratory testing for coagulation factors and the AT-III.

The aim of this study was to compare the coagulation profile of patients with RA with that of healthy controls. Methods. Ninety patients with RA and 90 healthy controls were recruited. Coagulation screening tests were performed, including prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and international normalised ratio (INR). Results. On comparison of the two groups, patients with RA exhibited a significantly reduced PT (12.5 vs 13.3s, p=0.03) and aPTT (25.1 vs 26.7s, p=0.01) with a significantly increased INR (1.19 vs 1.07, p<0.0001). Conclusion. Patients with RA have a distinct coagulation profile that is characterised by a reduction in PT and aPTT and an elevation in INR. Copyright © 2013 The Authors. All rights reserved.

The study was carried out by the University of Southampton and conducted in partnership with the University of Manchester, and University Hospitals Southampton.

The work was a multi-centre study, with researchers analysing data from blood tests taken from 1,558 patients diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis as part of the QUEST-RA study, a large international study investigating the safety and effectiveness of different rheumatoid arthritis treatments.

The researchers measured the levels of two proteins in the blood; high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) and N-terminal prohormone B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), which are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. They then compared these measurements with other large studies to provide more insight into the increased risk of cardiovascular disease in people with rheumatoid arthritis.

The results showed that levels of both hsCRP and NT-proBNP were significantly raised in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, indicating an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. The researchers also found that the levels of both proteins were correlated with disease activity, severity and damage to joints. HsCRP is a more established cardiovascular risk marker but NT-proBNP has gained importance in recent years as an independent marker of cardiovascular disease risk.

The study was led by Dr Georgina Taylor at the University of Southampton and Dr Rebecca Davies from the University of Manchester. Dr Taylor commented:

“We now know that people with rheumatoid arthritis have an increased level of these two proteins, which can then lead to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. We need more research in this area, but our next step would be to use these findings to see if there are certain subgroups of patients with rheumatoid arthritis who are at a greater risk of cardiovascular disease, and then to see if we can offer them specific treatments to help reduce this risk.”

Dr Davies added: “At the moment, we do not know which patients with rheumatoid arthritis are most at risk of cardiovascular disease, so this research would need to be followed up with a large, multi-centre study to investigate this. We also need to find out what the increased risk means for the long-term management of rheumatoid arthritis.”

It can impact the function of many body organs, including the lungs, heart, and skin. RA is a chronic condition, meaning there is no cure, and symptoms can come and go over time. The course of RA can be unpredictable, with periods of relative remission, or lack of disease activity, interspersed with periods of flares, or increased disease activity. The joint inflammation associated with RA can result in erosion of joint tissue, leading to pain, aches, stiffness, and loss of function. The condition can also lead to fatigue, fever, sweats, and loss of muscle tone. The exact cause of RA is unknown, but it is believed to be a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental triggers. RA can be challenging to diagnose, as its symptoms can be similar to other conditions. A diagnosis of RA is typically made based on a combination of medical history, physical examination, laboratory tests, and imaging studies. There is no known cure for RA, but there are various treatments available to manage the symptoms and slow the progression of the disease. These may include medication, physical therapy, exercise, and in some cases, surgery. Living with RA can be challenging, both physically and emotionally, but with the right support and treatment, many people with RA are able to manage their symptoms and lead active, fulfilling lives.

But why this is, has been a mystery until now.

Scientists at the University of Cambridge have discovered that a rogue enzyme in the BRAF gene – which is activated by the protein that causes the skin condition – is also responsible for the increased risk of CVD.

The team analyzed data from 603 patients with nevi maligna, a rare form of melanoma, and 1,723 people who did not have the disease. They found that those with the disease had a 50% greater risk of experiencing a CVD event like a heart attack or stroke, and were 1.6 times more likely to have experienced a CVD event at some point in their lifetime.

The team used a technique called CRISPR to modify the BRAF gene in cells, which allowed them to observe how the gene affected the function of blood vessels. They found that the gene activated an enzyme called PGE2, which causes the blood vessels to swell and become inflamed. The inflammation makes it more difficult for blood to flow around the body, increasing the risk of a CVD event.

The team also tested their theory by treating cells with a drug called Vorinostat, which stops the production of PGE2. This reduced the swelling and inflammation, and so the risk of a CVD event in patients with nevi maligna.

Dr. Mark Falone, one of the team at Cambridge, said: “Our findings open the door to new ways to treat patients with nevi maligna and reduce their risk of cardiovascular disease. Our next step is to investigate whether the same mechanism is at play in other forms of melanoma, and other cancers too.”

Dr. Silvia Coppi, the first author of the study, added: “We hope that our study will not only lead to new treatments for patients with nevi maligna, but also those with other forms of melanoma, and other cancers, which have been linked to CVD events.”

The team’s research was published in the journal Nature Communications.

The researchers believe that this is the reason why the blood clots in RA patients are more likely to cause a heart attack or stroke. 

The researchers also found that the thicker strands of fibrin were caused by an overproduction of two proteins called SERPINE1 and TAFI in the blood of RA patients. In a healthy person, SERPINE1 and TAFI work together with other proteins to help the blood clotting process. But in the case of RA, the excessive production of SERPINE1 and TAFI results in a delayed inactivation of SERPINE1, which causes the blood clots to form thicker and faster. 

The researchers used a mouse model to test their hypothesis. They injected blood from healthy mice and RA mice into mice with a different genetic background, which would otherwise have had a normal immune response. They found that the blood clots formed faster and were thicker in mice injected with blood from RA mice. 

The researchers also tested their hypothesis in a clinical study involving 71 healthy individuals and 76 RA patients. They found that the blood from RA patients was more likely to form blood clots than the blood from healthy individuals. 

The researchers believe that their findings could lead to new treatments for RA patients. For example, they believe that drugs that inhibit the production of SERPINE1 and TAFI could be used to prevent the formation of thick blood clots in RA patients. 

In the future, the researchers hope to test their hypothesis in larger clinical studies and to identify other factors that may contribute to the formation of blood clots in RA patients. They also hope to collaborate with other researchers to further explore the link between RA and blood clots.

The findings suggest that the changes in the blood could be a biomarker for the disease, according to the researchers.

"Although we have known for some time that the amino acid make-up of the blood fibrin in patients with RA is different from that of healthy people, we still do not know what causes the difference or what role it plays in the disease process itself," says study co-author Elisabeth Svensson, a rheumatologist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden.

The study appears in the journal Arthritis & Rheumatism.

Future studies should focus on whether the amino acid differences in the blood fibrins are a target for new treatments, Svensson adds.

For the current study, the researchers analyzed blood samples from 14 RA patients and 14 healthy controls. The samples were collected between 1990 and 1994 and all the study participants were women.

The researchers studied the amino acid make-up of fibrinogen — the protein that forms fibrin — in fresh frozen blood samples. Fibrinogen is a soluble protein; when a blood clot forms, the fibrinogen in the clot stabilizes and becomes insoluble and cross-linked fibrin.

To analyze the fibrinogen, the researchers used a technique called mass spectrometry to break the fibrin open and identify which amino acids it was made up of.

The researchers found that the amino acid make-up in the blood samples from RA patients differed in several ways from those of the healthy controls. The differences were most pronounced in two amino acids — glutamic acid and proline — and least pronounced in two other amino acids — valine and methionine.

The researchers also found that RA patients had less of one particular form, or isoform, of fibrinogen. This isoform has proline in the position that is usually taken by glutamic acid. As the number of isoforms influence how well-fibrin can perform its clot-stabilizing function, the researchers think this change might have some effect on the stability of blood clots.

The differences between the blood from RA patients and healthy people may be the result of the disease process itself, Svensson says. However, "it is also possible that the differences predate the disease and may represent a risk factor for development of RA," she says.

The authors of this study suggest that shared pathways between RA and CVD risk may present opportunities for RA treatments to have beneficial effects on CVD, and vice versa.

The researchers used a systems-biology approach to identify shared molecular signatures between RA and CVD. The systems-biology approach is complex and has been well-described elsewhere; it uses advanced computational analyses to identify patterns in large datasets. Here, the researchers applied this approach to gene-expression data from synovial tissue samples of RA patients.

They found that RA tissue samples had altered expression of genes associated with lipid metabolism, inflammation, and other CVD risk factors. These alterations were associated with the local tissue response to RA, rather than representing a systemic response to RA, since gene-expression changes were only observed in synovial tissue and not in blood. The researchers then validated these findings in two additional cohorts of RA patients.

Next, the researchers used the systems-biology approach to investigate the relationship between RA and CVD risk in more detail. They found that RA was associated with altered expression of genes associated with 13 of 21 established CVD risk factors. The researchers then tested whether these gene-expression changes were present in other rheumatic diseases, and found that they were not.

This study highlights the potential for future treatments that could target shared molecular pathways between RA and CVD. However, such treatments may be some time away. In the meantime, understanding the connection between these diseases may lead to improved CVD risk assessment and management for RA patients. For example, RA patients in this analysis with a family history of CVD, or those with persistently high rates of CVD biomarkers, may represent a high-risk subgroup who could benefit from increased monitoring and more aggressive CVD risk factor management.

Section 3 presents four case studies, while Sect. 4 discusses these in terms of the three objectives. In Sect. 5, we present the results of a questionnaire survey on perceptions of metocean forecasts. The usability gap is characterized by scientists’ preference for deep, technical information that may not be accessible to the public. The public, on the other hand, is interested in information that is easy to understand, relevant to their everyday lives, and that addresses their concerns and fears. To bridge this gap, scientists are encouraged to communicate more effectively with the public by explaining their research in a way that is understandable to non-experts. This can be done by using plain language, avoiding jargon, providing context, and explaining the relevance of the research to the public. Scientists can also consider using different formats, such as infographics, videos, or social media, to communicate their research to a wider audience. By doing so, scientists can help the public make informed decisions and become more engaged with science.

South Africa and Australia. The aim of this research is to develop an understanding of the importance of metocean information to coastal users in these countries, and to identify information needs that are not currently being met. The research was conducted in two phases. In the first phase, a literature review was conducted to identify information needs of coastal users in Australia and South Africa. This was followed by a survey of coastal users in both countries. In the second phase, interviews were conducted with coastal users in each country to gain a deeper understanding of the information needs that were identified in the survey. The study found that metocean information was highly salient to coastal users in both Australia and South Africa. Coastal users in both countries use metocean information to plan a range of activities including boating, swimming, surfing, beach going, and rock fishing. However, users also expressed a need for more and better information. There was a need for more detailed and specific information (e.g. real-time information; wave direction and height information; and tidal information) and a need for this information to be presented in a form that is more easily accessible (e.g. smartphone applications; information provided in advance; and forecasts that are easy to understand). The last point was particularly salient in South Africa, where many users expression a need for forecasts that are presented in a format similar to that used in Australia. This research has produced two primary findings. First, metocean information is highly salient to a range of coastal users in Australia and South Africa. Second, there is a need for more and better metocean information to be provided to coastal users in these countries, and for this information to be presented in a form that is more easily accessible. The research has contributed to an increased understanding of the importance of metocean information to coastal users in Australia and South Africa. The research has also contributed new knowledge about the information requirements of coastal users in these countries. The research provides a basis for future research into metocean information use by coastal users in these countries. The research will also assist coastal management authorities in Australia and South Africa to better understand the information needs of coastal users in these countries, and to better provide metocean information to coastal users. This will assist coastal users to make more informed decisions that may assist them to reduce their exposure to marine and coastal hazards.

The 17 posters will be displayed in a dedicated area in the main conference room and presenters will be available to discuss their work with conference attendees. The following are brief abstracts from the posters that will be displayed on Tuesday, November 5th, and Wednesday, November 6th, 2019.

Climate change and its impact on human health and health care

This poster discusses the impact of climate change on human health and health care. The authors also discuss the effect of extreme temperatures on health outcomes and health care utilization, the challenges to the healthcare system due to climate change, and the role of health systems in dealing with the health effects of climate change.

Usability and consistency of an ensemble postprocessor for regional climate change projections

This poster focuses on the development of an ensemble postprocessor for regional climate change projections. The authors address the issue of developing a user-friendly forecasting tool with a particular focus on ergonomics, accuracy and consistency, usability, and the display of uncertainty.

Evaluating the use of AHP for prioritising adaptation options for climate change in agriculture

The goal of this research was to evaluate the use of AHP for prioritising adaptation options for climate change in agriculture. The authors describe a pilot study in which AHP was used to prioritise climate change adaptation options at farm level in Zambia. The authors also discuss the relative importance of the different criteria used to prioritise the adaptation options and the robustness of the approach.

How can higher education institutions leverage their research to enhance their reputation in a highly dynamic and uncertain environment?

This poster explores the use of research to enhance the reputation of higher education institutions. The authors discuss their research on the reputation management of research-intensive universities and the challenges they face in enhancing their reputation in a highly dynamic and uncertain environment.

The use of climate information to improve community preparedness and resilience to climate extremes

This poster explores the use of climate information to improve community preparedness and resilience to climate extremes. The authors discuss a project that aims to improve public and private decisions by providing useful, location-specific, and seasonally appropriate climate information to help reduce vulnerability to extreme weather and climate events.

To build the framework, the research team used a combination of qualitative and quantitative research methods. The qualitative research included semi-structured interviews with key informants, open-ended questions during focus groups, and non-participant observations. The specific methods included participant-observer methods (Spradley, 1980; Spradley and McIntosh, 1997); in-depth interviews (Rubin and Babbie, 1998); and qualitative content analysis of focus group transcripts (Mayring, 2014). The participant-observer methods involved (1) participant observation with key informants (Spradley, 1980; Spradley and McIntosh, 1997) and (2) non-participant observation of ocean users' information interactions in three locations: commercial fishing vessels in Portland, OR, a recreational boating marina in Newport Beach, CA, and a naval base in San Diego, CA. The purpose of using a participant-observer approach was to gain a deeper understanding of how key informants and other ocean users make decisions. We defined a key informant as a knowledgeable person with first-hand experience at the activity or event being studied (Rubin and Babbie, 1998). For the recreational boating marina and the naval base, we observed information interactions at locations where ocean users gather information in person. The CCA was conducted in three steps. In step 1, a list of 18 statements was derived from the literature review and the findings of the qualitative interviews. These statements were evaluated in the quantitative survey. In step 2, the data from the quantitative survey were used to identify items for further analysis. Items were selected if they met the following criteria: (1) the absolute reliability (i.e. the number of individuals who answered the item divided by the total number of individuals who answered this item) was above 0.70; (2) the item had a significant effect in the regression model (p < 0.05); and (3) the effect size of the item was above 0.10. In step 3, new qualitative interviews were conducted among a smaller group of respondents (n = 12) until cultural consensus was reached. A cultural consensus was reached when the data met the following criteria: (1) above 0.70 absolute reliability for the agreement scale; (2) more than 85% agreement for all items in the consensus analysis; (3) no item with an effect size below 0.20; and (4) all individuals agreed on the ranking of the first three items in consensus analysis. The sample was selected through purposive sampling. The respondents were 495 men and women (aged between 18–60 years) who had been living in the study area for at least 12 months. Informed consent was obtained from each respondent. All respondents completed the quantitative survey. Of these, 425 respondents also completed semi-structured interviews in Nyaneka or Kimbundu, two major national languages in Angola. In-depth interviews were conducted with 20 additional respondents until data saturation was reached. All interviews were recorded. The quantitative data were analysed using STATA version 11.1. The qualitative data were analysed through open coding in NVIVO version 8. The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the Nuffield Centre for International Health and Development, University of Leeds, United Kingdom, and the Comissão Provincial de Bioética (Biology Ethics Commission) of Luanda, Angola. All interviewees received a small payment for their time.

First, the uptake of testing services is low in the early stages of the epidemic, but increases rapidly with the number of cases. Second, the uptake of contact tracing services is even lower than testing services. Third, the uptake of services is lower in areas with a higher proportion of older people. Fourth, the number of cases in an area is a better predictor of the number of people who use services than the number of deaths. Fifth, we find that the production of more accurate forecasts is possible, but this requires a significant increase in resources dedicated to the provision of testing and contact tracing services. Given that these services are labor intensive, a significant increase in the number of service providers would be required to produce more accurate forecasts. Finally, our results suggest that the production of salient forecasts in the early stages of an epidemic is not a luxury for rich countries, but is in fact essential in countries with fewer resources. This is because accurate forecasts allow for the allocation of limited resources to the most effective interventions, which is likely to have a greater impact in countries with fewer resources.

Each model is based on a different initial condition (a different guess as to how the atmosphere is moving) and each model produces a different forecast. A key factor in determining the accuracy of these forecasts is the accuracy of the initial condition.

The initial condition for a forecast is based on measurements of the atmosphere. In order to forecast the weather, one needs to know the current wind speed and direction, temperature, humidity, and pressure over the entire globe. These measurements are made by a variety of instruments, including weather balloons that rise into the atmosphere and drop a radiosonde (an instrument that measures wind, temperature and pressure) that transmits data as it rises, weather buoys that float in the ocean and make continuous measurements, weather stations on land that make measurements of the local weather, and weather satellites that make measurements of the entire Earth. All of these instruments make continuous measurements, but because the atmosphere is in a constant state of change, one cannot just take a single snapshot and use that to initialize a forecast. Instead, the measurements are used to initialize a forecast every few hours. The frequency of the initialization depends on the type of forecast. Global weather models are typically initialized every six hours while short-range models for a limited region (such as a single state) can be initialized every hour or more often.

The results of this study are published in the journal “Ocean & Coastal Management”.

“Coastal communities are often exposed to natural hazards, such as tropical storms or tsunamis, that can have devastating consequences,” explains Dr. Tom Spencer of the University of Plymouth. “We know that, increasingly, coastal communities around the world are turning to ocean forecasts to help them prepare for and respond to these events. But we don’t yet fully understand what information they are using, how often and how reliable it is.”

For their study, the scientists had questionnaires completed by 180 people in the coastal community of Beaufort, North Carolina and 100 people in the coastal community of Gansbaai, South Africa. The participants were asked how often they use ocean forecasts, what they are using them for and what factors influence their trust in the forecasts.

The results showed that the forecasts were used more frequently than previously thought. In Beaufort, for example, 44 percent of the fishermen said they check the forecasts every day or almost every day. In Gansbaai, 57 percent of the commercial fishers and 29 percent of the recreational fishers said they use the forecasts at least once a week.

The scientists were also able to identify factors that can improve the usefulness and acceptance of the forecasts. These include more detailed and precise forecasts as well as forecasts that are tailored to the specific needs of the coastal community and communicated in a way that is relevant to them.

“Coastal communities have unique needs when it comes to ocean forecasts,” says Dr. Scott Glenn of the Rutgers University in New Brunswick, USA. “By understanding what information they need and why, we can develop more relevant and useful forecasts for them.”

The scientists believe that their findings can help to improve existing forecasting services and develop new ones. “Our results show that there is a demand for the information provided by ocean forecasts,” says Spencer. “By understanding this demand, we can ensure that future forecasts meet the needs of the coastal communities that rely on them.”

Reference: “Understanding the use and trust in ocean forecasts by coastal communities” by Scott P. Glenn, Emily R. Ward, Thomas J. M. Spencer, Andrew P. Barnard, Rachel S. White, Lloyd W. Wright, Madgalena D. Flink, and James P. Casey, 19 January 2023, Ocean & Coastal Management.

In this study, we present a detailed analysis of the use of antibiotics in 42 Danish children, aged 0-16 months, admitted to a university hospital with a primary diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), and provide an in-depth description of the clinical characteristics of the patients, their laboratory values, radiographic findings, and clinical courses, with a focus on differences between children who received antibiotics and those who did not. Our results indicate that children with CAP have a high disease severity at admission to the hospital, with prolonged duration of symptoms, high rates of comorbidity, and a generally poor prognosis. Admission to the hospital and treatment with antibiotics were not associated with improved prognosis, although a trend towards better outcome was seen in children with the largest symptom-to-admission delay and in those admitted to the hospital early in the course of the disease. Early initiation of antibiotics was not associated with poorer outcome. The children in this study did not generally receive adequate fluid treatment or oxygen supplementation, although children who received antibiotics had higher central venous pressure and lower urine output than those who did not. The overall use of antibiotics was high and not associated with major differences in treatment or outcome between children who received antibiotics and those who did not. The most frequent antibiotics given were clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and clindamycin. Children who received antibiotics had more coagulopathy and higher levels of C-reactive protein and procalcitonin at admission than those who did not; however, the levels of these markers returned to normal more quickly in the antibiotic group. This is the first detailed description of the clinical course and treatment of children with CAP in Denmark and one of very few descriptions from countries in the Southern Hemisphere. The high disease severity and poor prognosis in the children in this study underline the importance of future studies of pneumonia aetiology and treatment in children in Denmark. Such studies are needed to develop strategies for both prevention and treatment of childhood pneumonia.

A Case Study in Northern Benin

The climate crisis is a global challenge that is particularly acute in the African Sahel region. In this context, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation-funded research project ‘Climate Smart’ developed a participatory method to assess the climate resilience of agricultural interventions in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Nigeria. This method uses a set of indicators to evaluate the progress of an agricultural intervention in adapting to the climate crisis. This article presents a case study that applies this method to an agricultural intervention in northern Benin. This participatory method helps to fill the gap in the evaluation of climate resilience in the Sahel and provides valuable insights for climate-smart interventions in the region.

samples.hyp:
-Control Study: A Population-Based Study of Schistosomiasis, HIV and Thalassemia in a Rural Community in Tanzania

This page is designed to provide a basic summary of a research project. It is not the full study and does not contain all of the researchers’ findings. This research was published in the journal PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases on January 20, 2016. You can view the full article online here.

What was the aim of the study?

The study aimed to describe the prevalence and identify risk factors of schistosomiasis and thalassemia in a rural community in Lushoto, Tanzania. Schistosomiasis is a parasitic disease that causes ill health, anemia and disability, and thalassemia is a genetic blood disorder. Both diseases are prevalent in the Lushoto community. The study also aimed to describe the prevalence of HIV and determine the relationship between schistosomiasis, thalassemia and HIV.

What were the methods of the study?

The study used a case-control approach. A case was defined as a person with evidence of current or past schistosomiasis or thalassemia. Cases were recruited from the health facilities and schools in the Lushoto community. Controls were defined as persons without evidence of current or past schistosomiasis or thalassemia. Controls were recruited from the Lushoto community.

The researchers collected data on risk factors by interviewing cases and controls. They used Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to visualise the geographical distribution of the cases and controls.

What did the study find?

A total of 484 cases and 480 controls participated in this study. Schistosomiasis was more common in males compared to females (male: 8.9%; female: 4.4%). Thalassemia was more common in females compared to males (female: 3.1%; male: 1.7%). HIV prevalence was higher in cases (11.0%) compared to controls (4.8%). Schistosomiasis was more common in areas with no water treatment compared to areas with water treatment. Thalassemia was not associated with any demographic factors. The researchers did not find any evidence of an association between HIV and schistosomiasis, or between HIV and thalassemia. However, the study had some limitations, including the use of school children as controls

This study aimed to identify and prioritise objectives for CSA in the context of South African grain farming. The objectives were identified through a literature study and interviews with agricultural advisors. The relative importance of the objectives was evaluated by means of a questionnaire survey among 98 grain farmers from the central grain producing areas in South Africa. The results of the study indicate that the most important objectives for CSA in the context of South African grain farming are: maintaining or improving soil health (e.g. through conservation agriculture practices); increasing the resilience of farming systems to deal with climatic risks and shocks (e.g. through the use of cover crops); and the use of grazing animals as an alternative to mechanical weed control. The results also indicate that objectives can be grouped into categories based on the type of farming systems and the scale of the farming operation. The study also indicates that the objectives can be grouped into enablers, performancers and result categories. The enablers category comprises objectives related to natural resource management and research, while the performers category comprises objectives related to farming practices and the result category comprises objectives related to off-farm and on-farm social and economic results. The objectives in the enablers and performers categories are considered to be input objectives, while the objectives in the results category are considered to be output objectives. The study further indicates that multi-cropping and minimum tillage are the most important CSA practices for small-scale farmers, while conservation reserves and controlled traffic are the most important CSA practices for large-scale farmers. The results also indicate that the CSA objectives are not very well known among grain farmers. Therefore, training and education on CSA are essential to ensure that the potential of CSA is realised among grain farmers in South Africa.

This is despite the fact that there is a rapidly increasing number of interventions that purport to be climate smart. This is also true for the case of agriculture, which is one of the sectors that is most vulnerable to climate change and at the same time is well positioned to make a major contribution to solutions.

The objective of this paper is to contribute towards filling this gap by presenting a set of criteria for assessing the climate smartness of interventions in the agriculture sector. The paper begins by defining climate-smart agriculture and then proceeds to develop criteria for assessing the climate-smartness of interventions. The criteria are discussed in three domains: 1) the policy and institutional domain, 2) the technology and practice domain, and 3) the impact domain. In the domain of policy and institutions we argue that climate-smart interventions should be based on legitimate and inclusive policies and institutions. In the domain of technology and practice we argue that climate-smart interventions should support adaptation and mitigation, be environmentally sound and be supported by advisory services. In the domain of impacts we argue that climate-smart interventions should have positive and significant impacts on productivity, on farmers’ income and on resilience.

samples.src: Here, we describe a new participatory protocol for assessing the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions in smallholder practices.
samples.ref: Ní ibí a mẹ́nu ba àwọn ìlànà ìkópa tuntun láti ní àǹfààní sí ìjáfáfá-ojú ọjọ́ ti ìdásí ètò ọ̀gbìn.láàárín àwọn alábọ́ọ́dé.
samples.hyp:
The framework is based on the principles of co-designing with farmers and the use of participatory methods. The climate-smartness of 24 interventions was assessed in four agro-ecological zones in Kenya. The interventions were assessed for their adaptation, mitigation, and resilience-enhancing potential by the farmers themselves. The climate-smart assessment was based on the following criteria: (i) the potential of the intervention to support farmers’ adaptation and resilience to climate variability and extremes, and (ii) the potential of the intervention to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The potential of the interventions to support climate change adaptation and resilience was assessed at two levels: at the level of the individual farm and at the level of the entire community. At the farm level, the assessment considered the type of intervention, its frequency, and the number of farmers who practiced it in a season. At the community level, the extent to which the intervention promoted community adaptation and resilience strategies was evaluated. The assessment of the potential of the interventions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions was based on the type of intervention and its frequency. The assessment methods included semi-structured interviews, seasonally-structured questionnaires, and seasonally-structured observations. The assessment was based on the number of times an intervention was practiced in a season, the number of farmers practicing it, the duration of the intervention, and the number of seasons the intervention had been practiced. The assessment criteria were considered critical for achieving climate-smart agriculture (CSA) objectives. The assessment approach can be used by researchers, extension workers, and development agents to prioritize and design climate-smart interventions.

The indicators were selected based on their relevance to the CSA theme and their availability in the literature. The indicators were also chosen to be representative of different disciplines, including economics, agronomy, sociology and environmental science. The indicators are presented in the three pillars of CSA: agricultural production, income and markets, and natural resources and the environment. For each indicator, the relationship between the indicator and food security, CSA, or climate change was described, and literature references were provided. In addition, we developed seven composite indices for the food security and adaptation pillars using the selected indicators. The indices were developed using principal component analysis (PCA). We used the indicator values from the 103 farms in the study by Delzeit et al. (2019) to calculate the indices. The composite indices provide a snapshot of the current situation regarding food security and adaptation to climate change from the perspective of smallholder farmers in the semi-arid Tropics. The indices can be used to quantify the food security and adaptation status of CSA practices in the region and to identify the areas where interventions could have the biggest impact.

samples.src: The protocol was tested among 72 farmers implementing a variety of CSA interventions in the climate-smart village of Lushoto, Tanzania.
samples.ref: Ìlànà yìí jẹ́ yíyẹ̀wò láàárín àwọn àgbẹ̀ 72 tí ó ń ṣe àmúlò oríṣi àwọn ìdásí ní àwùjọ Lushoto, orílẹ̀-èdè Tanzania tí ojú ọjọ́ rẹ̀ jáfáfá.
samples.hyp:
The average age of the participants was 48.3 years old (SD 12.1); 53% were female. Participants were exposed to the protocol in two different small group settings: a half-day workshop and a farmer field school (FFS) activity. Workshops were held over 12 months, and FFS took place weekly over the same period. We used a mixed methods approach to evaluate the impact of the protocol. Quantitative data were collected using farmer-led observations and a pre-test post-test design with control group. Qualitative data were collected using farmer-led observations, field notes, and semi-structured interviews with focus groups and key informants.
The results of the study showed that the protocol was effective in increasing farmers’ knowledge of CSA practices, changing farmers’ attitudes towards CSA practices, and increasing the number of farmers practicing CSA. The average knowledge scores increased from 11.2 (SD 2.7) at pre-test to 16.4 (SD 3.3) at post-test, p <.0001. There was a statistically significant increase in the use of different types of CSA after the intervention (Z = -4.711, p <.0001). Twenty-one farmers who had no previous experience with CSA practiced at least one type of CSA by the end of the study.
Farmers reported that the protocol was relevant, easy to understand, and easy to implement. The group exposure through the FFS was preferred because it provided an opportunity for “learning by doing.” The hands-on activities facilitated by the field practitioners were perceived to be the most relevant and valuable components of the protocol. The workshop inspired the participants to take action and create a community-based change agent, who in turn facilitated the FFS. This support from the community was crucial for the success of the CSA practices.
The study also showed some limitations. Not all the farmers who attended the workshop participated in the FFS. The control group did not have the same opportunity to discuss and learn about CSA compared to the groups that received the protocol. The activities of the control group were observed by research staff rather than farmers, which may have influenced the results. The location of the control group was far from the research site, and some farmers had to walk for over 2 hours one way to reach the research site. This made it difficult for them to participate in all the activities and take all the measurements. As a result, the control group had a high dropout rate.
The study identified some challenges to scaling up the use of the protocol.

samples.hyp:
The new techniques will help scientists and farmers prepare for climate change. Photo: Colourbox

New techniques can help reduce the effects of climate change. The techniques were developed together with farmers and other stakeholders in climate change monitoring. The results are described in the scientific journal The Crop Journal.

Climate change will have a huge impact on agriculture. For example, changes in the climate will bring new pests and diseases that can reduce the yield of crops. Therefore, new methods are needed to monitor the effects of climate change.

According to Associate Professor Signe Bergaust Holmberg at the Department of Mathematical Sciences at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), farmers and other stakeholders in climate change monitoring were involved in the development of the new techniques.

“These stakeholders are in direct contact with the fields. They know when the time is right to cut the grass or when it is time to plant potatoes. Through this involvement, the methods are more relevant for the users,” says Holmberg.

The new techniques focus on the development of a more precise calendar for when to plant certain crops. The calendar is based on weather data, which is used to estimate the correct time to sow different crops.

The methods also use weather data to estimate the risk of pests and diseases. The idea is that the methods will help reduce the use of pesticides and other measures to protect the crops.

The developed methods were tested in two case studies. Both studies were conducted in collaboration with Norway, where one study was conducted in collaboration with Kenya, and the other with India.

The methods were tested on four different crops: Wheat in Norway and Kenya, and groundnuts, also known as peanuts, in India.

According to Holmberg, the methods are generic and can be used for other crops as well.

“Farmers already use weather data to plan their work. But with these methods, they will be better equipped to adapt to the changing climate,” says Holmberg.

The Crop Journal

This method will help scientists and farmers in Africa and around the world work together to develop climate-smart practices that will be most effective in different locations and ecosystems.

The method was developed by scientists at the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) and the World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF), both members of the CGIAR, a global research partnership for a food-secure future. “There is a lack of evidence about what’s actually working in terms of improving smallholder productivity and farmers' incomes,” said Elizabeth Caraher, a social scientist at the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) who studies the adoption of climate-smart agriculture practices.

To address this gap, Caraher and her colleagues conducted a systematic review of 100 impact evaluations of climate change interventions targeting smallholder farmers in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The findings were published today in the journal Advances in Atmospheric Sciences.

Previous reviews of climate-smart agriculture impact evaluations have either focused on a small number of countries or evaluated interventions that focused on only one aspect of climate change, such as increasing crop yields, Caraher said. The review conducted by Caraher and her colleagues is the first to provide a comprehensive assessment of the effectiveness of climate-smart agriculture interventions that address multiple aspects of climate change, including water scarcity, extreme events, and increasing temperatures.

The researchers found that the most common outcome evaluated by impact evaluations was crop yield, Caraher said. However, the results were mixed, with some studies finding a positive effect and others finding a negative effect on yield. The reason for this, the researchers suggested, is that some interventions involved planting heat-tolerant crop varieties, while others exposed farmers to drought-prone varieties. The impact of planting heat- or drought-tolerant varieties on yield depends on whether these traits are associated with lower yields because of the specific climate in the study site.

The researchers also found that many impact evaluations relied on quantitative impact data alone, such as yield data, rather than using qualitative data, such as interviews with farmers, to better understand why an intervention may have succeeded or failed. “If you’re just looking at changes in yield, you could miss interventions that are successful in some places but not in others because of the specific weather conditions,” Caraher said.

Photo credit: A. Bala/CIAT

A new way to identify research priorities in collaboration with local stakeholders

Researchers at the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) have developed a collaborative approach to identify research priorities in a way that is acceptable, transparent, and builds trust with local stakeholders.

The researchers applied this method in the Lushoto district of Tanzania, a region known for high agricultural potential but also subject to frequent droughts. The aim was to identify research priorities for pearl millet and sorghum, two staple grains that are important for food security in the area, and which are also well-adapted to the region’s dry conditions.

The method had three steps. First, the researchers worked with experts to identify a list of 30 traits for pearl millet and sorghum that could be improved through research to increase crop yield, climate resilience, and other agronomic factors.

The second step was to prioritize these 30 traits through a series of focus group discussions with local stakeholders in Lushoto. The stakeholders discussed the importance of each trait and how likely it was that research to improve the trait would be useful. These discussions were facilitated by CIAT social scientists, with the support of local research institutes Ilonga and TARI, and the funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

In the final step, the team used a mathematical model to calculate the “utility” or usefulness of each trait, taking into account how important stakeholders thought each trait was, and how likely they thought it was that research on the trait would be useful. This resulted in a list of the top 10 priority traits for each crop that were accepted by both stakeholders and scientists.

The process was well-received by stakeholders in Lushoto. “Of the 30 traits we considered, the top 20 were selected by both the experts and the stakeholders, which was very impressive,” said Dr. Jennifer Cunrath, a social scientist at CIAT who worked on the project. “This shows that you can have agreement between the experts and the farmers on what are the most important things to work on. This is key to ensuring that the research is going to be useful,” she added.

The study, published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, describes how this process worked, and also includes the prioritization results so that other users can apply the method to their own research areas. The researchers plan to use this prioritization in planning new research trials for pearl millet and sorghum in Lushoto.

In the paper, the team describes the genome sequence of the Sudanese strain and compares it to other available SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences from around the world. They also performed a range of computational analyses to help understand the likely path the virus took as it spread through Sudan and the unique traits it acquired along the way.

The virus that causes COVID-19 is actually a family of related viruses. These viruses are constantly mutating, generating tiny changes in their genetic code that can affect how they spread and infect people. It’s important to characterise these mutations to understand the potential impact they could have on things like vaccine effectiveness and the efficacy of treatments.

The team’s analyses suggest that the Sudanese virus shares early mutations with viruses found in other countries in East Africa. It then picks up a unique set of mutations that distinguish it from viruses found in other parts of the world. One of these, the L452Q mutation, has been linked with increased transmissibility and is also found in the Indian variant of the virus.

The researchers also used the sequence to create a 3D model of the Sudanese virus. They found that it contains a set of spike protein mutations that may allow it to bind to and enter human cells more easily, although further research is needed.

“We’ve shown that the Sudanese virus is genetically distinct from other SARS-CoV-2 viruses and has evolved its own set of mutations. Some of these mutations have been linked with changes in how the virus spreads and how it infects people, so it’s important we continue to monitor its evolution as it spreads further,” says Nephishururu.

Invasive species are defined as species that are non-native to a region and exhibit one or more of the following impacts: economic (e.g. agriculture), environmental (e.g. biodiversity), human health (e.g. zoonoses), or ecological (e.g. habitat modification). Due to the diverse nature of these impacts, it is useful to consider invasive species from the perspective of different sectors. The pathogens of vertebrate animals are one such sector, and their impact is entirely ecological. The aim of this paper is to review the current knowledge on pathogens of vertebrate animals that have invaded new areas and ecosystems, with a focus on South Africa. This paper defines a pathogen as an invasive species that is non-native to an area or ecosystem, and is able to cause disease in the host species. Examples of such pathogens are discussed, with a focus on those that have been reported from South Africa, and those that have the potential to invade the country. The pathogens discussed include both those that infect wild vertebrate species (zoonoses), and those that infect domestic vertebrates. Examples of zoonotic pathogens discussed in this paper are those that have caused, or still cause, significant economic losses in South Africa, as well as those that have caused significant ecological changes. The pathogens that infect domestic vertebrates have been selected because they are able to spread to wild populations and cause disease in wild vertebrate species. Examples of such pathogens are foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), which has the potential to cause local and global extinctions of vertebrate species, and African swine fever (ASF), which also has the potential to spread to wildlife. The knowledge gaps and future research needs that can guide the management and control of these pathogens are also discussed.

The introduction of the Zebra mussel into the Great Lakes of North America is a prime example of the potential for introduced pathogens to do great ecological and economic harm. The Zebra mussel is a small freshwater bivalve that is native to Eurasia. It was accidentally introduced into the Great Lakes via ballast water from European and Russian ships. Once in the Great Lakes, it had no natural predators or competitors and it rapidly increased in numbers, outcompeting native species like the Quagga mussel (also introduced from Europe) and causing major ecological changes in the ecosystem. One of the major ecological changes caused by the Zebra mussel was the near elimination of native freshwater sponges. samples.hyp:
Source: University of California - Davis

Released: 11/18/2014 8:50:00 AM

Contact Information

Sharon Barbour

Media Relations Coordinator

916-445-3031

Scientists have identified the genetic fingerprints of dozens of microbes that cause disease in people and animals in South Africa.

The new database, or catalog, of microbial strains isolated from patients and animals in South Africa will help scientists develop new diagnostic tests and treatments for infections.

The database, published in Scientific Reports, is the first to detail the genetic characteristics of clinical strains of bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites isolated from patients and animals in South Africa.

"This open-access catalog is a unique resource for researchers in South Africa and elsewhere," said Edward Breiman, lead author of the study and research scientist at the One Health Institute at the University of California, Davis, School of Veterinary Medicine.

The database was created using microbial strains isolated from 1987 to 2013 from patients and animals by researchers at the National Institute for Communicable Diseases, a division of the South African Department of Health, and the University of Pretoria.

The researchers made sure the database would be a useful tool for scientists in South Africa by consulting with them, said Breiman.

"We asked them what information they needed and built the database to meet those needs," he said.

The database details the genetic characteristics of 92 bacterial strains, 36 viral strains, 44 fungal strains and three parasitic worms. It includes information about each organism's host, where in the body it was found and the illness it caused.

The database also includes information about the genetic fingerprints of the organisms. These fingerprints can be used to rapidly identify an organism and are useful in diagnosing infections and tracking the spread of disease.

The researchers focused on strains that cause acute, or short-term, infections. This focus should increase the chances that the database will lead to the development of new diagnostic tests and treatments, the authors said.

The database includes strains that cause pneumonia, meningitis, blood infections, gastroenteritis, septicemia, wound infections and genital infections.

"Because the strains in the database were isolated from patients and animals in South Africa, they are likely to be more relevant to the South African situation than strains studied elsewhere," said study co-author Dr. Somabile Masebo, a researcher at the University of Pretoria.

The database will be updated periodically to include new strains and those from other regions of South Africa, the authors said.

samples.ref: Nínú ẹ̀ka ìsèwádìí tí a ń pè ní ‘sáyẹńsì àfòmọ́’ àwọn onímọ̀ sáyẹ́ńsì ṣe ìwádìí àwọn ọ́gánísíìmù tí wọ́n máa ń fa ìpalára lẹ́yìn tí wọ́n bá ti yọjú sí agbègbè tuntun, níbi tí wọ́n kò sí tẹ́lẹ̀.
samples.hyp:
Invasive species are often used as models to study the impact of biological invasions on native species and ecosystems. However, the impact of invasive species on human health is not well understood. Here, we study the impact of the invasive western honeybee Apis mellifera on the demography of a native bee, the giant honeybee (Apis dorsata), in East Java, Indonesia. We use a unique combination of experimental and observational approaches. First, we introduce A. mellifera into six colonies of A. dorsata. Second, we use a statistical model to test whether the introduction of A. mellifera affects the survival or reproductive success of A. dorsata. Finally, we use paternity analysis to examine whether the competitive interaction between A. mellifera and A. dorsata is causing reproductive parasitism (where a genetically unrelated male sires the offspring of another bee). We find that the introduction of A. mellifera reduces the survival and reproductive success of A. dorsata. We also find that A. mellifera is successful in taking over nests of A. dorsata, and that the relatedness between workers and queens in take-over nests is lower than in undisturbed control nests, suggesting that reproductive parasitism is occurring. Our results show that the interaction between the two bee species has important consequences for the demography of native bees.

The global burden of disease is increasing, and invasive pathogens are a major factor. However, we know relatively little about the distribution of invasive pathogens in nature, and how this affects their impact. This project will characterise the distribution of invasive pathogens in a representative sample of nature reserves to understand how this affects their impact. The project will apply a new risk-assessment framework that takes into account the effects of invasive pathogens in competition with other pathogens and competitors. This will be achieved by combining field sampling with experiments at The Natural History Museum’s Biodiversity and Environmental Research (BER) department’s insect facility. The Natural History Museum’s insect facility has a unique capability to assess the fitness of individual insects by combining environmental scanning electron microscopy with nano-CT scanning and X-ray fluorescence. It is one of only a few facilities in the world that can provide this combination of high-resolution imaging and elemental analysis. The project will also engage with the public by holding family events at the Museum and by participating in the BBC’s Countryfile Live event.

The microbiota of animals and humans consists of the indigenous microorganisms that are necessary for a healthy state of the organism. The indigenous microbiota colonizes a large number of host sites such as the skin, the oral cavity, the urogenital tract, the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and the female genital and reproductive organs. The indigenous microbiota exists in a dynamic state of equilibrium with the host, which is called the commensal state and consists of a large number of microorganisms of the same kind but of different phenotypes that live in a symbiotic relationship with the host. The symbiotic relationship is based on a mutual benefit to the host and the microorganisms. The microorganisms obtain their energy and nutrients from the host, and the host obtains various vitamins and protection from the microorganisms against other microorganisms that can cause disease. The indigenous microbiota is passed vertically from mother to infant during and after childbirth, and it is also passed horizontally between individuals of the same species.


Each microorganism of the indigenous microbiota has its specific location or niche in which it lives. The GI tract is the main target of microbiological research and is the best-studied part of the indigenous microbiota. The GI tract consists of the mouth, the pharynx, the esophagus, the stomach, the small intestine, the large intestine, and the anus. The microorganisms that colonize the different parts of the GI tract have different nutrient sources and environments and therefore have different phenotypes. The microorganisms of the oral cavity are mainly involved in dental caries and periodontal diseases, and they obtain their energy from complex carbohydrates, such as starch and glycogen. The microorganisms of the pharynx and the esophagus are mainly involved in tonsillitis and esophagitis and obtain their energy from mucin. The microorganisms of the stomach are mainly involved in gastric ulcers and gastrointestinal tumors and obtain their energy from the breakdown products of blood cells. The microorganisms of the small intestine are involved in inflammatory diseases, such as coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and Crohn’s disease. A prospective analytical study was conducted on 52 patients diagnosed and treated for OK between the years of November 2017 to November 2021 in the department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, College of Dental Sciences, Sultan Quaboos University, Muscat, Oman. The data was analyzed using SPSS version 3.3.

Out of the 52 patients, 36 (69.23%) were males and 16 (30.77%) were females with age range of 8 to 18 years. Keratocyst was seen more commonly in the third decade with 29 (55.77%) cases. Gingiva was the most common site accounting for 39 (75%) cases, followed by floor of mouth with 5 (9.62%) cases. Enucleation was the most common surgical procedure performed, which was done in 26 (50%) cases followed by en bloc resection in 20 (38.46%) cases. The mean follow up period was 43.1 months. Recurrence was seen in 7 (13.46%) cases during the follow up, which was higher in cases treated by enucleation (5/26 = 19.23%) as compared to en bloc resection (2/20 = 10%). Complications were seen in 3 (5.77%) cases.

Conclusion: OK is a cyst with high recurrence rate and treatment modalities like enucleation and en bloc resection provide good cure rates, however, higher recurrence rate was seen in cases managed by enucleation as compared to en bloc resection.

Although it is the most common cystic lesion of the jaw, accounting for 3% of all jaw lesions, and 60% to 70% of all jaw cysts, the behavior of OKC is unpredictable and can be locally aggressive.
The mainstay of treatment for OKC is en bloc resection, but this can make it difficult to determine the adequate margin. Positive margins can be managed with additional surgery, but there is no consensus on the need for adjuvant radiotherapy for negative margins. Select cases may be managed with curettage and cauterization, but the behavior of the lesion and the need for long-term follow up make this approach less favorable for most cases.
The biology of OKC remains under investigation. The underlying oncogenic pathway in OKC has not been identified, and there is no proven molecular marker for recurrence or aggressiveness. β-catenin is a known driver of the pathway in other lesions, but is not consistently overexpressed in OKC. Recent evidence suggests that the overexpression of a microRNA-217 as a downstream target of β-catenin may be a diagnostic marker for OKC, but its role in the pathogenesis is unknown. Further investigation of the molecular biology of OKC is needed to identify the underlying oncogenic pathway and develop a reliable molecular marker for recurrence and aggressiveness.
The most common site for OKC is the mandibular symphysis in young adult males, and this association has led to the concept of an “aggressive OKC”. It has been suggested that these aggressive OKCs have a higher rate of recurrence after conservative treatment, but the available evidence is limited to two small case series. One group found a recurrence rate of 58% at 5 years in patients treated with curettage and cauterization, while the other found a recurrence rate of 35% at 13–59 months in patients with positive or uncertain margins that were managed with either curettage and cauterization or en bloc resection. The role of histologic features in predicting the behavior of OKC is unclear. Some have suggested that the presence of cystic and papillary areas are associated with more aggressive behavior, but this has not been validated.

The main goal of this review was to summarize the literature regarding the treatment of odontogenic keratocyst and provide an overview of the current management options. PubMed and Embase were searched to identify studies on the treatment of odontogenic keratocyst. The search was restricted to studies published between January 1980 and December 2018. Studies were selected if they described the treatment of odontogenic keratocyst. A modified version of the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale was used to assess the risk of bias in all selected studies. A total of 19 studies were included in the synthesis. Most of the included studies were retrospective in nature. There was a lack of high-quality randomized controlled trials. Cystectomy with or without postoperative irradiation was found to be the most commonly performed procedure. Other treatment modalities that have been used with variable success rates include cryosurgery, caustic ablation, cryoadhesion, and laser ablation. The clinical behavior of OKC is highly unpredictable and treatment options may vary depending on the size of the lesion, number of cysts, and recurrence rate.

A team of researchers from the University of Malaya (UM) has suggested a few ways to improve the treatment of jaw disease.

The team’s study, published in the Journal of Oral Pathology and Medicine, showed that the current treatment for jaw disease may be limited by the availability of healthy jaw bone.

Jaw bone is often affected by a chronic disease known as Nonsyndromic Osteonecrosis of the Jaw (ONJ), which is a condition where the bone in the jaw starts to die and leads to severe pain and disability.

The team’s study suggested that the combination of a tissue-stimulating factor and a vascular endothelial growth factor could regenerate the jaw bone and that this combined factor could be used to regenerate bone in other parts of the body as well.

The team’s co-leader, Associate Professor Dr. Lai Fong Wong, said that the current treatment for jaw bone loss is a surgical reconstruction with bone grafting and placement of dental implants.

However, the surgery may be difficult to carry out due to the lack of healthy jaw bone, which in turn may lead to multiple surgical procedures, additional costs, and longer treatment times.

The study also suggested the use of a biodegradable scaffold with the combined factor as a potential treatment for jaw bone loss.

Dr. Wong said that the next step would be to carry out preclinical studies on animals to test the efficacy and safety of the combined factor.

The UM team’s study was a collaborative effort between the School of Dental Sciences and the School of Medicine with the University of Malaya.

The team’s co-leader, Professor Dato’ Dr. Khalil Shaharom, said that the study showed how researchers from different disciplines can come together to work on a problem that affects public health.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 has infected over 400,000 people globally. To prevent such infectious diseases, a vaccine is urgently needed. In this study, we designed a synthetic vaccine for SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV by using the most conserved regions of the spike (S) protein as epitopes. To identify the most immunogenic and cross-reactive epitopes, one hundred in silico ligands were docked against the most conserved regions of the S protein of 105 SARS-CoV-2 strains. We performed a comparative epitope analysis of SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV by using bioinformatics tools. The results of the epitope prediction for SARS-CoV-2 showed that most of the predicted epitopes were located in the N-terminal domain of the S protein, particularly in S1 domain. We also evaluated the T cell epitopes for all three viruses by using 29 HLA class I alleles. The results of this study will be useful in the future design of a synthetic peptide vaccine, which could be further improved by adding one or more glycans to the peptide epitopes.

In this study, we have developed a recombinant viral vector based vaccine candidate against covid-19 using a plant derived virus that has been used in many other vaccine applications. The virus used is a heterologous plant virus, which does not infect humans or animals and is safe. This covid-19 vaccine candidate is a recombinant virus that does not replicate in culture and is designed to express a fusion protein consisting of the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 linked to the full length hemagglutinin protein of influenza virus. The preclinical studies show that the virus is immunogenic and protection is achieved in mice against a heterologous challenge with a mouse adapted strain of SARS-CoV-2. The vaccine candidate will be further evaluated in non-human primates and if successful, a clinical trial will be designed to test the safety and immunogenicity in humans.

The human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I and class II molecules interact with peptide antigens generated from pathogen proteins to elicit a T-cell response. Peptide binding to HLA class I is primarily evaluated by its binding affinity to the most common HLA class I allotypes expressed in the population. However, HLA class II molecules bind peptides in a groove at the center of the molecule and peptide binding to HLA class II is much more complex. Therefore, HLA class II binding epitopes were selected based on multiple parameters including the ability to bind to frequent HLA class II DRB1 allotypes, location of the peptide in the pathogen protein and its immunogenicity. The candidate epitopes were tested for their immunogenicity in mice and for their ability to protect mice against lethal challenge with the live virulent strain of the respective pathogen.
