Scientists around the world are racing to understand the virus behind the Covid-19 pandemic, and how to treat it.

The disease is caused by a coronavirus that was first detected in December 2019 in Wuhan, China. The number of cases has since risen exponentially, and the World Health Organization declared the outbreak a global health emergency on 30 January 2020.

Here’s what we know so far:

What is a coronavirus?

Coronaviruses are a large family of viruses that can cause illness in animals and humans. In humans, coronaviruses can cause respiratory, gastrointestinal and neurological diseases.

New coronaviruses can emerge from time to time, but four have caused major outbreaks in recent decades.

They are:

  • Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS): This coronavirus epidemic caused severe respiratory symptoms in humans and was first reported in China in 2002. The disease killed about 774 people, mostly in China and Hong Kong.
  • Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS): First reported in Saudi Arabia in 2012, MERS causes severe respiratory symptoms and has a high fatality rate. It kills around 35% of those infected, and has been found in people in more than two dozen countries.
  • The current Covid-19 pandemic. This coronavirus causes Covid-19, which can cause a range of symptoms in humans, from a mild flu to life-threatening pneumonia. It was first detected in December 2019 in Wuhan, China. As of 25 March, there were more than 470,000 confirmed cases and over 21,000 deaths due to Covid-19.
  • There is no specific treatment or vaccine for Covid-19, but the symptoms can be treated individually, as they would be for the common flu.

What is still unknown?

Scientists still don’t know much about Covid-19, but they are working around the clock to find out more about it.

Here are some of the questions they are trying to answer:

  • How did the virus emerge?

samples.hyp:
The study aimed to present the pooled estimates of prevalence and risk factors of new-onset arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.

This systematic review and meta-analysis was performed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines. A search was conducted in PubMed, EMBASE, and SCOPUS for studies reporting the prevalence of arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19, up to November 2020. Data extraction and quality assessment of the included studies were performed. The main outcome was to calculate the pooled prevalence of new-onset arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19, and to identify the risk factors for arrhythmias in these patients. Stata version 530, ECDC (version 5.4.1), and R-statistics (version 3.6.2) software were used.

A total of 24 studies with 20,701 participants were included in the study. The pooled prevalence of arrhythmias was 16.1% (95% CI 13.6–18.6%). The prevalence of arrhythmias was higher in studies with moderate to severe disease compared to those with mild disease (21.7% vs. 9.3%, p < 0.001). In patients with arrhythmias, first-degree heart block was the most prevalent (8.1%) followed by atrial fibrillation (6.8%), ventricular tachycardia (5.3%), and bundle branch block (4.3%). In the multivariable analysis, increasing age (OR 1.17, 95% CI 1.11–1.23, p < 0.001), diabetes (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.46–3.49, p < 0.001), chronic kidney disease (OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.32–3.32, p = 0.002), and C-reactive protein level ≥ 75 mg/L (OR 2.01, 95% CI 1.32–3.06, p = 0.002) were significant risk factors for arrhythmias.

The prevalence of arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 was 16.1%. Increasing age, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and CRP level ≥ 75 mg/L were identified as risk factors for arrhythmias in these patients.

This study aimed to summarize the current understanding of the prevalence, mechanisms, and impact of cardiac arrhythmia in COVID-19 patients.
A systematic review was conducted in the PubMed, EMBASE, and SCOPUS databases until July 2020. The search terms included “arrhythmia” OR “cardiac arrhythmia” OR “heart block” AND “COVID-19” OR “2019 novel coronavirus” OR “SARS-CoV-2”.
A total of 17 studies were included in this review, with a study sample size ranging from 5 to 273 patients. The median age of the patients was 58 years. The overall prevalence of cardiac arrhythmia in patients with COVID-19 was 20% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 14%-26%). The most prevalent arrhythmia was atrial fibrillation, which was recorded in 7 studies with a prevalence of 7.3% (95% CI: 4%-11%). The second most common arrhythmia was bradycardia, which was reported in 5 studies with a prevalence of 8.9% (95% CI: 4%-14%). The prevalence of other types of arrhythmia was as follows: ventricular tachycardia (4.4%, 95% CI: 2%-7.9%), bundle branch block (3.2%, 95% CI: 2%-4.7%), third-degree heart block (1.8%, 95% CI: 1.1%-2.9%), and ventricular fibrillation (1.4%, 95% CI: 0.5%-2.3%). In addition, the prevalence of arrhythmia was significantly higher in severe and critically ill patients with COVID-19 than in mild and asymptomatic patients. This study also found that about half of the patients with cardiac arrhythmia in the COVID-19 setting had no known history of cardiac arrhythmia prior to admission. Moreover, 36 non-synonymous mutations were identified in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the spike protein with a low prevalence (<1%) across all genomes, of which only four could potentially enhance the binding of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein to the human ACE2 receptor. In addition, patients with cardiac arrhythmia had a higher risk of all-cause in-hospital mortality, longer length of hospital stay, and lower rate of discharge.

Many Covid-19 patients had irregular heartbeats during infection, study finds
Photo: Shutterstock

People who tested positive for Covid-19 were more likely to have irregular heart rhythms or heart flutters during their infection than people without the virus, a new study finds.

The analysis of more than 2,600 patients also showed that those with pre-existing heart conditions were more likely to experience these types of heart complications during infection.

The study was published online Nov. 18 in the European Heart Journal.

“Many patients had heart rhythm disturbances that were not present before they developed Covid-19,” said lead study author Dr. Jonathan Pearson, a cardiology fellow at the University of Utah School of Medicine in Salt Lake City.

“These findings are important because heart rhythm disturbances associated with Covid-19 may not only cause symptoms that make patients feel ill, but they can also have serious consequences if not recognized and treated appropriately,” Pearson said in a university news release.

For the study, Pearson and his colleagues analyzed data from 2,657 patients in the U.K. who were hospitalized with Covid-19.

All of the patients underwent an electrocardiogram (ECG) while they were in the hospital. An ECG is a test that measures the electrical activity of the heart.

The researchers also analyzed ECG data from a group of 5,328 patients who did not have Covid-19. These patients were recruited from 142 general practices that were part of the U.K.’s QResearch program. This program provides access to patient medical data for research purposes.

The researchers found that 20% of the Covid-19 patients had new-onset atrial fibrillation or flutter. These are types of heart rhythm problems that involve an irregular heartbeat. The most common symptom is a rapid and irregular pulse.

The risk of heart rhythm disorders was about 1.5 times higher for Covid-19 patients than for those without the virus.

The risk was even higher for patients who had existing heart conditions, the researchers reported. About 30% of these patients developed an irregular heart rhythm during their illness.

Patients with Covid-19 also had a higher risk of developing heart rhythm disorders if they were older, if they were currently or formerly smokers, or if they had high blood pressure or diabetes.

The researchers also found that patients who had heart rhythm disorders before they became infected with SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes Covid-19, were at the greatest risk of developing more serious heart complications.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the prevalence of cardiac injury in Covid-19 patients and its association with the severity of the disease. We also assessed the relationship between cardiac injury and clinical characteristics, laboratory parameters and outcome of Covid-19.

This was a retrospective observational study of Covid-19 patients admitted to four hospitals in Wuhan between February and April 2020. Cardiac injury was assessed by measuring the levels of cardiac troponin I (cTnI), with levels above 40 ng/L defined as cardiac injury. The primary outcome was the occurrence of arrhythmia and the secondary outcome was the occurrence of cardiac death, as well as the length of hospital and intensive care unit (ICU) stay, and whether patients required mechanical ventilation.

Of the 64 patients included in this study, 59 patients (92%) had elevated cTnI levels. Patients with cardiac injury were more likely to be non-survivors (46% vs. 16%), require ICU admission and mechanical ventilation (56% vs. 16% and 60% vs. 17%, respectively), have lower levels of lymphocytes, higher levels of CRP, D-dimer and IL-6, and more often have severe disease (84% vs. 16%). Patients in the cardiac injury group had a longer hospital (19 vs. 13 days) and ICU stay (13 vs. 8 days) compared to patients without cardiac injury. Multivariable regression analysis showed that cardiac injury was an independent predictor of the need for mechanical ventilation (OR 8.63, 95% CI 2.44-30.26), and of death (Hazard ratio 5.40, 95% CI 2.13-13.80).

Our study showed a very high prevalence (92%) of cardiac injury in hospitalized Covid-19 patients. Cardiac injury was associated with increased disease severity, more laboratory abnormalities, a longer hospital and ICU stay, and worse outcome. These findings suggest that, in addition to respiratory failure, cardiac dysfunction may contribute to a significant portion of Covid-19 mortality.

We begin by briefly describing the global context of migration and mental health. We then present the results of studies on the prevalence of PTSD and other mental health outcomes in migrants. Next, we provide a review of studies examining the association between migration-related variables and mental health outcomes in migrants. We conclude by highlighting some of the methodological issues and recommendations for future research.

Keywords: Migration; mental health; PTSD; wellbeing; risk factors; protective factors.

1.1. Migration and mental health

There are two main reasons why mental health is a particularly salient issue for migrants. First, migration is a stressful process [1,2]. Migration typically involves multiple changes, including economic, social, cultural and political changes [3,4]. For many migrants, there is also the added pressure of having to adapt to a new cultural environment and finding employment in a new country [5,6]. Migration can also impact the social networks and support available to migrants, with research showing that migrants are more likely to experience social isolation and loneliness compared to non-migrants [7,8,9]. However, a few studies have suggested that post-migration stressors have a larger impact on the mental health of migrants and refugees. The current study aimed to investigate the relative impact of pre- and post-migration stressors on the mental health of a sample of Arab refugees who were hosted in the Palestinian society, and to examine the moderating effect of gender and duration of residence on the relationship between stressors and mental health. The sample included 437 Arab refugees (mean length of residence = 15.05 years, SD = 9.46 years). Results of multiple regression analyses indicated that post-migration stressors had a significant impact on the mental health of the participants. In addition, the length of residence had a moderating effect on the relationship between stressors and mental health. Specifically, for the early stage of acculturation (i.e., for refugees who spent the first 5 years in the host country), stressors had a negative impact on the mental health of the participants. However, for the later stages of acculturation, stressors had a positive impact on their mental health. Furthermore, the results indicated a moderating effect of gender on the relationship between stressors and mental health, such that stressors had a more negative impact on the mental health of women, compared with men. The findings are discussed in the light of the most recent theories on migration and mental health.

English:
The transition from one country to another can cause a range of mental health issues for refugees, according to new research.

The study, published in the journal Social Science & Medicine, found that the process of leaving an individual’s country of origin and settling in a new country can have a significant impact on mental health, regardless of the circumstances in a refugee’s home country.

The research, led by Dr Olaf Köpke from the University of Southampton, examined data from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) relating to 34,000 refugees across 25 countries.

It found that refugees who had been in their new country for less than five years were more likely to have symptoms of anxiety and depression. Those who had been in their new country for longer were more likely to have thought about dying, have an eating disorder and have been detained.

The researchers say the findings suggest that the situation an individual is fleeing and the experience of settling in a new country are important factors which can impact on mental health.

The study also found that men were more likely to have symptoms of anxiety and depression, while women were more likely to have thought about dying and to have been detained.

Dr Köpke, from the University of Southampton’s Centre for Disaster Medicine and Humanitarian Health, said: “The results suggest that the situation an individual is fleeing and the experience of settling in a new country are important factors which can impact on mental health. The findings also highlight the importance of including mental health in the care of refugees, particularly in the first few years after arrival in a new country.”

Professor Steffanie Knorr from the University of Southampton’s Institute of Mental Health said: “The results of this study add to a growing body of literature on the mental health of refugees. The findings have important implications for policy and practice and highlight the need for tailored mental health interventions that address the multiple challenges that refugees face across the lifespan.”

The research, published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, also noted high rates of suicide ideation and attempt among young people with a history of war experiences and migration. The studies included data from the United States, United Kingdom, and Israel and involved nearly 1,600 young adults.

“[Our] results support the notion that adverse experiences associated with war and migration confer risk for major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and suicidal ideation and behavior among young help-seeking refugees,” wrote the authors. 

For the purposes of the study, major depressive disorder was defined as frequent episodes of sadness and/or loss of interest in activities once enjoyed, along with other symptoms such as changes in appetite and sleep patterns, fatigue, and feelings of worthlessness or hopelessness. 

Generalized anxiety disorder was described as six months or more of feelings of constant and overwhelming worry and concern. While PTSD is often associated with military veterans, anyone who has experienced a traumatic event, such as sexual or physical assault, can develop the condition. 

The researchers also noted that almost a third of the refugees in their study met the criteria for alcohol use disorder (AUD). 

“Refugees are at elevated risk of developing both substance use and mental disorders, which often co-occur in migration contexts,” they wrote in their paper. 

Although previous research has examined the mental health of young migrants and refugees, the authors noted that this is one of the few studies to look at the specific group of young people who are aged 18 to 25 and have sought help for their mental health.

samples.ref: Ìwàláàyè àti ìtẹramọ́ Amblyomma Hebraeum ń fa àfikún sí wàhálà àwọn àìsàn tí ìdun ń fà sí ara àwọn ẹran ìsìn ní Àgbègbè Gúùsù Botswana
samples.hyp:
Heartwater is a tick-borne disease of cattle, caused by the protozoan parasite, Ehrlichia ruminantium. The disease is transmitted by the brown ear-tick, Amblyomma hebraeum. The study area comprised the southern district of Botswana. The study used a cross-sectional survey of cattle and their ticks. A total of 1870 adult A. hebraeum were collected from 225 cattle. The overall tick infestation rate was 18.89% and the disease prevalence was 2.2%. The odds of infestation were 12.57 times higher in cattle with heartwater infection than in cattle without the infection. The infection was more likely in females than males. The odds of infestation were 2.9 times higher in cattle with high tick burden than in those with low tick burden. The odds of infestation were 3.4 times higher in cattle with high tick burden and heartwater infection than in those with low tick burden and without heartwater infection. The high prevalence of infection of A. hebraeum and the high tick infestation rate increase the risk of transmission of heartwater in the study area. The high prevalence of heartwater in cattle with high tick burden will result in the persistence of the disease in the area. Thus, tick control should be intensified in order to reduce the risk of heartwater transmission.

The disease is caused by the rickettsia Haemoplasma (H.) musebeii, which is transmitted to livestock by the brown ear tick, Amblyomma variegatum. The objective of this study was to determine the prevalence of H. musebeii in cattle and to identify the risk factors associated with the infection. A cross-sectional study was conducted in cattle from five villages in the Ngamiland West District of Botswana. A total of 520 cattle from 104 herds and 26 farms were examined for the presence of antibodies against H. musebeii using the indirect meat spot test. Data on management and production practices were collected by means of a structured questionnaire. The overall prevalence of heartwater was 7.1% (37/520). Antibodies against H. musebeii were more common in cattle >2 years of age (p < 0.0001) and in cattle with clinical signs (p = 0.03). Cattle from farms with >50 cattle (p = 0.03) and herds with >25 cattle (p = 0.01) were more likely to be infected. The number of cattle that were treated for ticks in the 30 days prior to sampling was significantly lower (p = 0.02) in positive herds compared to negative herds. Heartwater is endemic in the study area. Infection was significantly associated with age, clinical signs, farm size and herd size. The results of this study suggest that the application of age- and tick treatment-related strategies may be used to reduce the transmission of H. musebeii in the study area.

samples.hyp: Heartwater is a disease of domestic ruminants caused by the protozoan parasite, Klossella spp. which is transmitted by the brown ear tick, Rhipicephalus everti. The epidemiology of the disease is influenced by a number of factors including the distribution of the parasite and the tick, the climatic conditions, host resistance and control measures. In this study, the distribution of the parasite and the tick, the prevalence of the disease, the clinical signs, the seasonality of the disease, the pattern of sero-conversion and the tick burden are investigated in cattle and sheep in Botswana. In addition, the efficacy of acaricide impregnated ear tags in controlling tick infestations on cattle and sheep under field conditions is studied. A cross-sectional study design was used to determine the prevalence and the distribution of the parasite and the tick. A total of 364 sheep and 614 cattle from 20 villages in the study area were examined for the presence of K. spp. and R. everti. In the serological survey, 1134 sheep and cattle from 22 villages were tested for the presence of antibodies to K. spp. using the indirect haemagglutination assay. A total of 1539 sheep and cattle from 26 villages were used to determine the tick infestation levels on experimental animals treated with acaricide impregnated ear tags compared to those treated with blank tags. The results indicated that heartwater is enzootic in the study area. The overall prevalence of Klossella spp. in cattle and sheep was 5.2% and 2.5%, respectively. A higher prevalence was observed in cattle than in sheep. The overall prevalence of the tick, R. everti was 5.2% and 0.8% for cattle and sheep, respectively. Sero-prevalence of heartwater in cattle and sheep was 44.0% and 18.6%, respectively. The clinical signs observed in infected animals included anorexia, depression, fever, lameness, arrhythmia and heart failure. The disease occurred throughout the year, but the peak occurrence was during the hot-dry season. Sero-conversion was more frequent in young animals less than two years of age. The tick burden was high throughout the year, but the peak tick counts were during the hot-dry season. The mean number of ticks per infested animal was 11.8, 8.2 and 6.

The information gathered was used to identify the main constraints and problems in the control of the disease. The results of this study indicate that the disease is still a major constraint to livestock production in the study area. This is reflected in the low level of compliance with the recommended control measures. The main reasons cited for the low level of compliance with the recommended control measures were a lack of time to implement the measures, a lack of belief in the effectiveness of the measures, and a lack of communication between the researchers and the farmers. The lack of time to implement the recommended control measures is a major constraint to the integrated control of heartwater in northern Nigeria. This is because the control measures are labour intensive and are carried out during the cropping season when labour is in high demand in both the agricultural and the pastoral communities. The lack of belief in the effectiveness of the control measures used for the integrated control of heartwater is a major constraint to the successful implementation of the measures. This lack of belief is a serious problem which has received little attention in the literature. The major recommendation of this study is that the attention of all stakeholders in the control of heartwater should be focused on the problem of a lack of belief in the effectiveness of the recommended control measures among the farmers. Further research is recommended to identify the factors that contribute to the lack of belief in the effectiveness of the recommended control measures among the farmers. These factors should be investigated with the aim of developing strategies for their removal in order to achieve high levels of compliance with the recommended control measures for the integrated control of heartwater in northern Nigeria.

The disease is widespread in West Africa, and is sometimes referred to as African animal trypanosomiasis to distinguish it from human sleeping sickness.

The disease is caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Trypanosoma, transmitted by the bite of an infected tsetse fly. T. vivax and T. congolense each cause severe disease in cattle, goats, sheep, camels, and other domesticated animals, whereas T. brucei gambiense causes human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness). T. evansi causes mild disease in dogs, and has also been isolated from other animals including pigs, rats, and monkeys. T. simiae has also been isolated from cattle, and has been associated with severe disease in cattle, water buffalo, and sheep.

The trypanosomes then infect the blood of the victim. The disease is called heartwater because the parasites accumulate in the heart and nearby blood vessels, reducing the amount of blood the heart can pump. This causes a build-up of fluid in the brain, breathing problems, and a high body temperature. The high temperature causes the animal to stop eating, and eventually die from starvation and infection.

Study reveals how a single malaria infection can boost risk of subsequent infection

The researchers were based in Botswana. (Image: Unsplash)

A new study from the University of Bern, in Switzerland, has revealed how a single malaria infection can boost the risk of subsequent infections by 40%.

The research, published today in Science Advances, suggests that the elevated risk is due to changes in the human immune system’s response to malaria infection.

The study was led by Dr. Ritha Khoma, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Bern’s Institute of Immunology, in collaboration with researchers from the Botswana–Harvard AIDS Institute (B-HAI) and the Botswana Malaria Elimination Programme (BMEP).

“We know that malaria can cause a person’s immune system to become hyperreactive—a state known as a ‘hyperinflammatory syndrome’,” says Dr. Khoma. “This hyperinflammatory syndrome has been linked to asthma and other allergic diseases, as well as severe disease following vaccination.”

To reach their findings, the researchers used blood and urine samples collected from 101 children aged between 2 and 14, living in the malaria-endemic northwestern region of Botswana. The children were divided into three groups: 32 who had had two episodes of malaria, 36 who had had one episode, and 33 who had never had malaria.

The researchers then tested the children’s blood and urine samples for malaria infection, as well as immune responses to three common infections: influenza, pneumococcus, and tetanus.

Influenza and pneumococcus are bacterial infections, while tetanus is caused by a toxin produced by a bacterium.

The results showed that the children who had had one episode of malaria were 1.5 times more likely to show a immune response for a second infection, compared to those who had never had malaria. This effect was not seen in children who had had two episodes of malaria.

The children who had had one episode of malaria were 1.4 times more likely to mount an immune response against influenza, and three times more likely to respond to tetanus. Once again, no such increased response was seen in the children who had had two episodes of malaria, compared with those who had never had malaria.

samples.hyp:
Point of care testing (POCT) is a growing field in the field of diagnostic testing. By providing rapid, critical information, POC testing can significantly impact patient outcomes. However, barriers to the implementation and use of POC tests have been noted in many regions worldwide. This article aims to highlight the barriers to POC testing in India and South Africa.

In India, several factors contribute to the challenges of implementing POC tests. One major barrier is the country’s healthcare infrastructure. Many remote areas in India lack basic medical facilities, let alone the infrastructure to support POC testing. Additionally, cultural factors such as the preference for seeking second opinions from multiple doctors can hinder the effectiveness of POC testing, as patients may be more inclined to wait for confirmatory tests rather than rely on immediate results.

South Africa presents its own set of challenges. The country’s healthcare system, although advanced in comparison to many African nations, is still grappling with issues of inequality and access. POC tests are often not covered by medical aids or public health insurance, making them unaffordable for many South Africans. Moreover, the complex regulatory environment and requirements for POC testing devices can be overwhelming for healthcare providers, deterring their adoption.

Overcoming these barriers requires a multi-pronged approach. For India, improving healthcare infrastructure, especially in remote areas, is crucial. This could involve training healthcare workers in rural areas on how to effectively use POC tests and providing the necessary equipment. Additionally, raising awareness about the importance of POC testing and working with local communities to address cultural barriers can be beneficial.

In South Africa, increasing access to POC tests by working with medical aids and the public health insurance system, and providing financial incentives could make them more affordable. Simplifying the regulatory process and working closely with healthcare providers to understand their concerns and address them can also speed up the adoption of POC testing.

In conclusion, both India and South Africa face significant barriers to the implementation and use of POC tests. By addressing these barriers, which vary by region, we can enhance access to critical healthcare information, leading to improved patient outcomes and healthcare systems.

The project analyzed how the social and political context shaped the practices of diagnosis, the information produced, and the impacts of these on the lives of people living with chronic diseases.

The project used the concept of “diagnostic justice” as a framework to analyze the social, political, and economic implications of diagnostic practices. Diagnostic justice was conceptualized as going beyond mere access to diagnosis, in order to ask questions about the quality of diagnostic practices and the justice implications of the information generated through diagnostic practices. The project also developed the concept of “diagnostic ecologies” to analyze the interactions between actors, technologies, and infrastructures involved in diagnostic practices. In addition to providing an in-depth analysis of diagnostic practices, this project provided evidence-based recommendations for improving diagnostic practices and outcomes in low-resource and middle-income countries.

The project was led by Dr. Neelam Sachdeva and Dr. Preet Kaur Gill in collaboration with Dr. Sarah Atkinson, Prof. Anna Self, Prof. Sarah Haworth, Prof. Ian Jones, and Dr. Anna Williams. The project was funded by the Economic and Social Research Council (ES/R008744/1) as part of the Peace and Security Research Programme (2018-2021). The findings of the project were published in peer-reviewed journals, working papers, and book chapters.

The project team was based at the School of Geography and the Environment at the University of Oxford. The project worked with the following partner organizations in India: Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE), Jaipur, Rajasthan; Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), Dehradun, Uttarakhand; and Sangeetha Performing Arts, Chennai, Tamil Nadu. samples.ref: Nípa àwọn ìtumọ̀ àìsàn tó le gan-an àti ìtọ́jú àìsàn tó le gan-an nípa lílo ìtúpalẹ̀ èrò
samples.hyp:
: A methodological study

The concept of critical illness and critical care is used in several different ways, which makes it difficult to interpret and compare studies in this area. Therefore, concept analysis could be used to clarify the concept of critical illness and critical care. The aim of this study was to describe the methodological aspects of a concept analysis on critical illness and critical care. The method was developed by Walker and Avant. The concept was analyzed using a hybrid modifi ed Walker's method with a combination of the following steps: (1) purpose statements, (2) attribute identification, (3) casuistic analysis, (4) casuistic comparison, (5) logical crosswalk, (6) a description of related and unrelated concepts, and (7) a model of the concept. The analysis was conducted in five steps: (1) a literature search regarding the concept of critical illness and critical care, (2) analysis of the concept, (3) validation of the concept with content experts, (4) a new literature search to ensure that the concept was described correctly, and (5) a re-analysis of the concept. The analysis was conducted between 2014 and 2017. The results were presented in three parts. In the first part, the results from the literature search were presented. In the second part, the analysis of the concept was presented, and in the third part, the validation of the concept was presented. The literature search identified 376 sources and the risk of bias was considered low. A total of 29 experts were included in the validation. The experts had a median of 15 (11–22) years of experience and were from 12 different countries. The experts were asked to rate the extent to which they agreed with a total of 42 statements. More than 75% agreement was found for 33 statements and the I-CAM was 0.84. The experts also wrote open-ended comments. The comments were classified as being supportive, not supportive, or not applicable. The majority of the comments (70.7%) were supportive. The analysis identified 12 attributes and one antecedent and three consequences. The hybrid modifi ed Walker's method is suitable for concept analysis in critical care. The analysis provides a better understanding of the concept of critical illness and critical care and can be used as a basis for future collections of data in this area.

A conceptual analysis was conducted of 44 relevant, peer-reviewed publications that described the concepts’ application in healthcare. The majority of included publications were opinion pieces (n=30, 68.2%). The majority of participants (n=17, 38.6%) working in Australia or North America defined “critical illness” as “the acute illness leading to admission to, or receipt of treatment in, an intensive care unit”. In contrast, the majority of participants (n=19, 43.2%) working in Europe defined it as “severe disease leading to a high risk of mortality and/or life-threatening organ dysfunction even with the best available treatment”. No preference was evident for any particular definition amongst participants from other regions. For “critical care”, the majority of participants (n=18, 40.9%) working in Australia or North America defined it as “intensive care unit treatment or management”. Participants from Africa (n=4, 50.0%) and South America (n=6, 37.5%) most commonly defined it as “intensive care unit treatment or management delivered by/under the supervision of intensivists”. Participants from Europe (n=7, 41.2%) most commonly defined it as “intensive care unit treatment or management according to/consistent with international guidelines”. No preference was evident for any particular definition amongst participants from other regions. These findings suggest that there is a lack of consensus on the definitions of “critical illness” and “critical care” on a global scale. To move forward in a manner that avoids unnecessary confusion, we propose preliminary definitions for these concepts until a consensus is globally agreed.

samples.hyp:
The most commonly used definition of critical illness is that it is an illness that acutely causes, or is likely to cause, a life-threatening abnormality in the function of one or more organ systems. The definition implies that a patient with a critical illness requires urgent specialist care and monitoring in an intensive care unit (ICU). Critical illness can be thought of as a continuum of illness severity, from less severe (e.g. acute respiratory distress syndrome) to more severe illness that may require extracorporeal membrane oxygenation or mechanical support. This definition of critical illness is useful for epidemiological studies and for health services research, including outcome and resource use studies. However, this definition is not helpful for clinical studies, where it is useful to have a definition that also incorporates the concept of acute illness. As such, for clinical studies, a more useful definition of critical illness is that it is an illness that causes life-threatening severe acute illness, requiring specialist care and monitoring in an ICU. This definition is also useful for clinical practice and teaching.

The major strength of this study is that detailed clinical information was collected through medical record review and patient interview at a single institution by a study team experienced in clinical research on SCA. This is in contrast to previous studies in which data were obtained from death certificates or hospital discharge summaries which are not optimized for detailed clinical information.21, 22, 23, 24, 25 In addition, the present study included a large number of patients, which made the sample more generalizable. However, the study is limited in that it was conducted at a single center, and thus, the patients described may have some characteristics different from patients at other centers. Also, because of the retrospective nature of the study, detailed information on some patients was not available, and these patients were excluded from the final analysis. Finally, this study was not designed nor am I powered to look at survival.

The prevalence of SCA in this study was higher than previous reports, which may be related to the large number of patients from a single center. As our study was carried out over a 10-year period, future studies should examine whether the prevalence is increasing or decreasing.

in the nursing literature. The study was conducted in two phases. In phase 1, 15 articles published between 1989 and 1998 on the history and development of critical care nursing were reviewed. In phase 2, 12 electronic searches were performed to identify articles published between 1998 and 2004 that related to the concepts of critical illness and critical care. A total of 104 articles were reviewed. No single definition of critical illness or critical care was found in the nursing literature. Critical illness was defined in medical literature as a disease process associated with severe acute illness, presence of a life-threatening physiologic derangement, or failure of at least two organ systems. Critical illness is characterized by an acute, dramatic, and sudden onset; severe symptoms; high mortality rate; and overall reduction in a patient's physiologic function, which may progress rapidly. Critical care is defined as the comprehensive nursing care that is given to a patient with a severe physiological disturbance or a patient whose life is, or is at, risk. Critical care is a subspecialty of nursing and is also referred to as intensive care and intensive nursing. The scope of critical care includes the medical and nursing management of a patient with a severe physiological disturbance. The patient receives care from a specialized team of nurses and doctors in an intensive care unit. The patient's physiological function is continuously monitored and supported by mechanical devices. The setting of critical care may be an intensive care unit, a coronary care unit, a pediatric intensive care unit, a neonatal intensive care unit, or a special care unit. The provision of critical care requires specialized skills and competencies that extend beyond the scope of general medical and surgical nursing.

The study, published today in Critical Care, found that the number of patients classified as “critically ill” in the United States is higher than previous estimates and that the number of patients classified as “not critically ill” is lower than previously thought.

The study was conducted by researchers from the Johns Hopkins Center for Big Data in Health, the Johns Hopkins University School of Nursing, the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and the Johns Hopkins Hospital. They used 2016 National Inpatient Sample data from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, which included information from more than 44 million patient hospital stays across the United States.

The researchers re-defined “critically ill” to include patients who received life-sustaining procedures, such as mechanical ventilation, kidney dialysis or a heart monitor. They found that 19.1% of patients were critically ill, almost 10 percentage points higher than previous estimates. Patients who were not critically ill comprised 80.9% of patients.

The re-defined categories had a significant impact on the total number of patients and case mix for hospitals and health systems.

For example, Johns Hopkins Hospital’s estimated number of critically ill patients increased from 2,600 to 3,300, an increase of 27%. The estimated number of non-critically ill patients decreased from 10,400 to 9,700, a decrease of 7%.

The re-defined categories also had a significant impact on the case mix of patients at the hospital. The percentage of total patient days occupied by patients who were critically ill increased from 11% to 15%. The percentage of total patient days occupied by patients who were not critically ill decreased from 89% to 85%.

“By re-defining the categories of critically ill and non-critically ill patients, we were able to better understand the needs of our patients and how best to serve them,” says Priya Noria, M.D., assistant professor of nursing at the Johns Hopkins University School of Nursing and the study’s lead author. “This information helps us to allocate our resources more effectively and to provide the best care possible for all of our patients.”

The study, led by Dr. Shigeki Watanabe from the University of California San Diego, used data from the Intensive Care National Audit Project (ICNAP) and the American College of Critical Care Medicine (ACCM) to create a list of 59 terms that could be used to describe the care received by patients in intensive care units (ICUs). The terms cover all aspects of patient care, including diagnostics, treatment, and administration of medicine. The researchers then tested the terms on 20 doctors from seven countries. 

The doctors were asked to rate each term’s clarity, and whether they had ever used it before. The terms were also tested on ICU nurses and medical students. The researchers found that the doctors had the highest agreement ratings for terms related to administration of medicine (such as “drip, continuous” or “cannula, percutaneous central venous”), and the lowest agreement ratings for describing diagnostic tests (such as “chest radiograph” or “chest computed tomography”). 

The researchers hope that adopting standard definitions will improve the quality of patient care. “The use of uniform language descriptions of patient care is essential for meaningful comparison of patient populations, and for sharing information on clinical trials and patient-level data,” they wrote in their paper. 

Although most doctors around the world understand each other’s medical terms, they use different terms to describe certain aspects of patient care. The researchers say that this can make it harder to communicate about treatment and share data. The terms they developed are a step towards creating a universal language for medicine that all doctors can use worldwide.

The current definition of critical illness is “a life-threatening organ failure,” according to the authors of the paper published online today (April 8) in the Journal of Critical Care. But this definition may be contributing to a negative feedback loop in which patients give up on their lives, become depressed, and stop fighting their illnesses. 

“We need to change the way we think about critical illness,” said study co-author Quynghuy Tran, an intensive care physician at the University of Melbourne in Australia. “We need to focus on the fact that these patients may get better.”

To support their argument, the authors of the paper point to research showing that when people are told they are in the late stages of a terminal illness, they may start giving up on living and, as a result, they die sooner. This effect has been observed in patients with end-stage cancer, ALS, and heart failure. 

The authors also highlight the potential for new treatments, which aim to restore organ function in patients with critical illness. These treatments are still being tested, but they believe these experimental therapies may one day help patients turn their illness around. 

The authors call for a re-evaluation of the way end-stage critical illness is discussed in hospitals so patients know they still have a chance of survival. They suggest replacing the term “critical illness” with “severe illness getting better or worse,” and they think patients should be told their condition is severe but that they have a chance of recovery. 

“[The patient] should be told that they are sick but that there is hope,” Tran said. 

Tran said it’s too early to tell whether or not these changes in terminology will make a difference in patient care. But he hopes that by changing the way doctors talk to their patients, and by focusing on the small chance of survival, critical illness patients will fight harder to stay alive. 

“We want to give them that energy, that motivation to fight that bit longer,” Tran said.

Abstract
Background The obligate intracellular parasite Plasmodium infects liver cells of its mammalian hosts. Following invasion, the pathogen escapes the phagosome by remodeling the endo-plasmic reticulum (ER) into a non-fusogenic organelle, the PVM. To complete its life cycle, the parasite changes the microtubule (MT) organization of the infected liver cell, a feature of which is a distinct MT-based structure called the MT-based apical complex (APC). The APC is a dynamic structure involved in vector transmission, as well as in ER-to-PVM export, and MT-dependent motility of PVM components. The exact temporal and spatial regulation of MT changes during infection is unknown. Methods We performed the first genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen to identify host factors required for efficient alteration of MT organization in human cells by the malaria parasite Plasmodium yoelii 17XL. Results We identified 21 genes essential for P. yoelii 17XL infection of HepG2 cells, some of which are known to be involved in MT-associated functions and/or cellular trafficking. Interestingly, we identified CENPJ, a known γ-tubulin complex component essential for MT dynamics, as a factor essential for both MT changes and formation of the APC. We verified these results in human and monkey cell lines and during infection of non-human primates by P. berghei. samples.hyp:
Scientists have long known that when a malaria parasite infects a human liver cell it stays inside a small compartment.

Now, in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the University of Melbourne and the University of Bern have revealed how the parasite manipulates the cell to live in this compartment.

Lead author Dr. James Whittle, from the University of Melbourne, said the parasite changes the structure of the cell to form a compartment it can hide in.

“This compartment is like a bubble within the cell and allows the parasite to stay hidden from the immune system, and also to reprogram the cell to make more parasites,” Dr. Whittle said.

The researchers believe this is the first time this mechanism has been identified.

“We believe this is the first time this mechanism has been identified, which is exciting because it means we have found a new way the parasite is able to evade our immune system,” Dr. Whittle said.

The parasite uses a protein called subtilisin to make this compartment. When the researchers blocked the action of subtilisin, the parasite was no longer able to form the compartment and was killed by the liver cell.

Co-author Professor Michel Dumas, from the University of Bern, said the study has shown how the parasite adapts to survive in a specific environment.

“This adaptation allows the parasite to complete its life cycle and maintain the vital step in the transmission of the disease from human to mosquito,” Professor Dumas said.

The research is part of a broader international collaboration, the European Research Council Malaria Global Systems (MalGriS) project, which brings together scientists from 11 countries.

Professor Carlow, from the University of Melbourne, said this collaboration was crucial to have the expertise to study the parasite while in the liver.

“Malaria is a very complex disease and the parasite is able to infect many different types of cells and go undetected,” Professor Carlow said.

“We hope our findings will inform the development of new treatments and control measures to rid this disease, which poses a significant public health challenge in many parts of the world.”


  • Dr. James Whittle, Postdoctoral Fellow, The University of Melbourne
  • Professor David Carlow, Professor, The University of Melbourne
  • Professor Michel Dumas, Professor, University of Bern

“Parasites are not humans; they don’t have their own food sources and they don’t have their own metabolism,” said Dr. Ivan Dikic, professor at the University of Freiburg’s Institute of Biochemistry. “They use the cell machinery of their host organisms and they hijack it for their own purposes.” 

Dr. Dikic and his team focused on a particular group of proteins that are involved in transporting vesicles, which are packages of proteins and other cellular components that need to be shuttled across the cell. The host cell usually transports these vesicles to specific destinations, but the researchers found that when infected by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii, the cell sends the vesicles to the vacuole, the parasite’s holding container, instead. 

The researchers then discovered a protein called Rab5 and Rab34 that the parasite uses to reprogram the vesicles’ final destination to the vacuole. Rab5 and Rab34 are members of a family of proteins called Rab GTPases, which are known to be involved in vesicle transport. The parasite modifies these Rab GTPases to hijack the host cell’s transport system. 

The researchers then did a computer-based screening for small molecules that could interfere with the function of Rab5 and Rab34. They found a small molecule that interfered with the function of Rab5 and successfully blocked the transport of vesicles to the vacuole, which significantly reduced the growth of the parasite. 

“Small molecules that interfere with the function of Rab GTPases have been developed for a variety of other diseases, and our study provides a basis for further developing such drugs to be used against Toxoplasma and other intracellular parasites,” said Dr. Dikic. 

The researchers’ next step will be to test the molecule on a different strain of the parasite and to test the molecule’s effectiveness on parasites that have become resistant to available drugs. 

Dr. Dikic said it could take years to confirm the molecule’s effectiveness in animal models, but if successful, it could become a new anti-parasitic drug.

The most effective way to prevent infection is to treat mosquito nets with an insecticide. However, the insecticide chlordecone, which was used in the past, is still detected in the environment and in human bodies. It is therefore important to understand how long the insecticide persists in different parts of the body, and to investigate whether it can affect the function of sperm.

We studied the impact of chlordecone on sperm in a group of French West Indian men, who were exposed to the insecticide during their childhood. We measured the level of chlordecone in each man's blood and semen samples, and tested the sperm's ability to move and fertilise an egg.

We found that chlordecone is present in the blood of almost one in three of the men in our study at concentrations above the level at which effects on sperm function begin to occur. In the men with the highest levels of chlordecone in their blood, the concentration of chlordecone in semen was 12 times higher than in those with the lowest levels. There was no significant relationship between the time that had elapsed since the last known exposure to chlordecone and the level of chlordecone in either the blood or semen. Sperm mobility was significantly reduced in the men with the highest levels of chlordecone, and the ability of the sperm to fertilise eggs in the laboratory was also reduced in this group.

Our results suggest that chlordecone exposure continues to affect a man's sperm for many years after the last known insecticide treatment. As most chlordecone is carried in blood from the liver to the rest of the body, our results suggest that chlordecone may also persist in other organs that are important for reproductive health, such as the brain, where it could affect behaviour and decision making. Men and boys with the highest levels of chlordecone should be monitored, and further research is needed to confirm whether exposure to chlordecone has wider effects on fertility and reproductive health.

The use of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS) are the most important methods for reducing malaria morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa. However, the widespread and continued use of these tools has been challenged by the emergence of insecticide resistance in disease vectors. This is a particular concern for Plasmodium falciparum, the most deadly species of the malaria parasite. The Anopheles gambiae complex is the main vector of P. falciparum in sub-Saharan Africa. The high levels of selection pressure due to wide-scale use of insecticides for ITNs and IRS have led to the development of resistance in this vector. The cytochrome P450 (CYP) multidrug resistance (mdr) gene was first described in An. gambiae in 2000, and since then many studies have reported associations between CYP6P3 (one of the CYP mdr genes) SNPs/haplotypes and resistance to insecticides in this vector.

samples.ref: Ṣíṣàfihàn àwọn ohun abẹ̀mí sí agbègbè tuntun gẹ́gẹ́ bíi ipa ìwádìí ìyípadà lágbàáyé ní South Africa.
samples.hyp:
South Africa, like many other countries, is experiencing rapid environmental change as a consequence of global change. One of the drivers of global change is the spread of alien species. Biological invasions are a serious threat to native biodiversity, as well as to human health and economic interests. There is an urgent need to develop and apply methods for the management of biological invasions. In order to train personnel in the research methods required for this task, the Biological Invasions Working Group (BIWG) was established as a component of the South African Global Change Research Programme (SAGCRP). The group consists of a multi-disciplinary team of researchers from various institutions. The main objective of the group is to train postgraduate students from South Africa and from other countries in the research methods required for investigations into biological invasions. The group also undertakes research in the area of biological invasions with the aim of developing methods for the management of biological invasions in South Africa. The group has established collaborative links with various national and international institutions that are involved in research and management of biological invasions.

We identified 688 publications, from which we extracted information on species invasions (pollution and CO2 excluded); species abundances; trophic level; body mass; and carbon and nitrogen stable isotope ratios. Using these data, we examined biogeographic patterns of change, including changes in species composition and in trophic level, abundance, and carbon and nitrogen stable isotope ratios of biotic communities across South African ecosystems. We found that changes in community stable isotope ratios were better explained by changes in biotic abundances than by changes in species composition. The latter was better explained by changes in trophic level. In terrestrial ecosystems, mean trophic level increased between 2000 and 2018 (10.1% to 11.6% higher, p < 0.05), and in marine ecosystems, mean trophic level did not change significantly (−0.1% to 1.7% higher, p > 0.05). In contrast, mean carbon stable isotope ratios were higher in marine than in terrestrial ecosystems and increased in marine ecosystems (7.3% to 13.3% higher, p < 0.05) but not in terrestrial ecosystems (−1.4% to 0.6% higher, p > 0.05). In marine ecosystems, mean nitrogen stable isotope ratios were higher than in terrestrial ecosystems and increased between 2000 and 2018 (2.0% to 3.7% higher, p < 0.05), as did mean carbon to nitrogen ratio (5.2% to 8.3% higher, p < 0.05). The higher trophic levels, carbon stable isotope ratios, and nitrogen stable isotope ratios in marine compared with terrestrial ecosystems suggest that marine ecosystems are more affected by the drivers we investigated. We did not find evidence, however, that any of these drivers significantly affected marine or terrestrial ecosystems between 2000 and 2018.

samples.hyp: This study aims to address this research gap by investigating the effects of multiple stressors on demersal fish assemblages in the South African marine environment. As such, this study will provide a better understanding of the effects that multiple stressors have on ecosystems in South African waters, and provide insight into how these effects may be influencing the structure of demersal fish assemblages in this environment. In order to achieve this, a multidisciplinary approach is required, and the information gathered from this study will incorporate data from multiple research fields. In this study, a hierarchical analysis will be applied to investigate how different combinations of stressors influence the structure of demersal fish assemblages. A hierarchical analysis is required in this study as it allows for the investigation of how different stressors, and different combinations of stressors, influence demersal fish assemblages at multiple spatial scales. This study will assess if global climate change variables have a significant influence on demersal fish assemblages, and if local stressors (i.e. anthropogenic stressors) have a significant influence on demersal fish assemblages, both in isolation and in combination with climate change variables. The local stressors considered in this study are: (1) Choking species, (2) trawl discards, (3) trawling intensity, (4) trawl bycatch, (5) eutrophication, (6) ocean acidification, (7) sea surface temperature, (8) sea surface salinity, (9) primary productivity, (10) secondary productivity, (11) Benthic inorganic nutrient concentration, (12) Benthic organic nutrient concentration, (13) hard bottom substrate, (14) fished vs. unfished, and (15) depth. In order to assess how combinations of stressors influence demersal fish assemblages, a hierarchical analysis will be applied to data from five study sites (Cape West Coast, Namibia, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape, and Western Cape), which have different combinations of global climate change variables and local stressors. The five study sites have different combinations of global climate change variables and local stressors (Figure 1), which will allow for an investigation into how different combinations of stressors influence demersal fish assemblages. In this study, three global climate change variables will be assessed: (1) sea surface temperature, (2) sea surface salinity, and (3) ocean acidification.

In a recent systematic review, the proportion of research on invasive species in South Africa was found to be 9.5%, which is just below the global average of 11.3% (Fig. 1). However, while the research output on invasive species in South Africa is substantial, the majority of these studies are at the species distribution modelling (SDM) or biological control level. Studies at the policy implementation level are scarce, and studies that focus on the application of policy instruments to address invasive species are yet to emerge in South Africa. This is concerning because the more we know about the threat posed by invasive species, the better equipped we should be to manage this threat. In this review, we examine the current status of research on invasive species in South Africa and provide recommendations for future research and management.

The research presented here is based on a literature review and a desk study of 123 studies that have been conducted between 1980 and 2012 (Fig. 1a). We reviewed the literature on the interactions between invasive species and other agents that affect ecosystem engineering by native and non‐native species in freshwater habitats. We focused on biotic interactions, including predation, competition, herbivory, facilitation and antagonism, including their implications for ecosystem engineering and biotic interactions. We found that non‐native species can have indirect effects on native species via changes in the abundance and composition of resources (e.g. through changes in water clarity), but also through changes in the resource base (e.g. through changes in substrate stability). These changes can affect the interaction type and characteristics that are important for ecosystem engineering, such as facilitation. Indirect interactions can also affect the temporal dynamics of the system. This review also highlights the importance of including multiple stressors, and the temporal dimension, as well as multiple trophic levels, when studying these types of interactions. Finally, we suggest future research directions to further investigate these interactions.

Excerpt from the project description
The impact of biological invasions, climate change, and human activities on the environment is one of the most dramatic and destructive challenges facing the world today. Unfortunately, the combined effect of these stressors has rarely been investigated, even though research has shown that the negative effects of one stressor can be amplified by the presence of another stressor.

This international project is collaborative research between South African and repute international researchers, led by Professor Colin Biggs from the University of Queensland, and co-led in South Africa by Professor Colleen Downs from the University of KwaZulu-Natal. The project builds on existing strong research partnerships and infrastructure in each country.

The project will use a novel approach to map the combined effect of these three key stressors on South Africa’s ecosystems. The novel aspect of this work is the space-time subsetting of the three types of stressors (i.e. spatial coverage and extent, and temporal duration) so that the most synergistic combinations can be identified and prioritised for effective management. Further, the different types of stressors will be addressed using novel approaches and data sources. The project team will develop a research-into-action agenda to support environmental management in South Africa. The team includes experts in invasive species, climate change, biodiversity and conservation, and social-ecological systems. The research will have strong links to environmental management and the South African research and management community, and will provide training and capacity building for the next generation of researchers and managers.

The project will contribute to the protection and improvement of South Africa’s biodiversity, freshwater systems and natural resources. But the number of papers is not reflected in the implementation of policies to deal with the problem, they say.

A team of researchers led by the University of Pretoria (UP) and including South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) scientists, conducted a review of invasive species research published between 2000 and 2014 in South Africa.

The review was published in the journal Neobiota and reveals that of the 684 papers published in this period, 16% were done in partnership with non-academic institutions, 12% were community-based and 4% were co-produced by researchers and communities. The researchers say this is not enough and call for much greater collaboration between scientists, policy-makers and other stakeholders.

The review also shows that research has mostly focused on impacts and control of species - with only 31 papers looking at the governance structures put in place to deal with invasive species, and only one paper focusing on the implementation of policies.

The team included researchers from UP, the South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI), the University of Cape Town, the University of KwaZulu-Natal, and Rhodes University.

What are the natural drivers of global change?

The natural drivers are the natural processes that change the Earth system, and they include:

  • Changes in the Sun’s heat and light output, which are the main drivers of climate change.
  • The movement of tectonic plates, which creates mountain ranges, causes earthquakes and leads to volcanic eruptions.
  • The water cycle, which is the continuous movement of water above, below and through the Earth’s surface.
  • The rock cycle, which is the continuous movement of rocks within the Earth’s crust and between the crust and the mantle.
  • The carbon cycle, which is the movement of carbon between the biosphere and the atmosphere, oceans, land surfaces and rocks.
  • The oxygen cycle, which is the movement of oxygen between the atmosphere, oceans, land surfaces and atmosphere.
  • The nitrogen cycle, which is the movement of nitrogen between the atmosphere, oceans, land surfaces and atmosphere.
  • The Earth’s life cycle, which is the development and changes in life on Earth, and how it affects the chemical and physical processes of the planet.
  • The Earth’s climate cycle, which is the natural changes in the planet’s weather over time.
  • The Earth’s geological cycle, which is the development and changes in the planet’s surface over time.
  • The Earth’s biological cycle, which is the development and changes in the planet’s living organisms over time.
  • The Earth’s chemical cycle, which is the development and changes in the planet’s chemical processes over time.
  • The Earth’s physical cycle, which is the development and changes in the planet’s physical processes over time.

What are the anthropogenic drivers of global change?

The anthropogenic drivers are the changes in the Earth system that are caused by human activities, and they include:

  • Climate change, which is the natural process of the Earth’s climate system changing over time, and is caused by natural drivers.
  • Deforestation, which is the destruction of forests for agriculture, logging, mining, urbanization and other human activities.
  • Habitat fragmentation, which is the destruction of habitats by human activities, and is often caused by deforestation.
  • Habitat loss, which is the destruction of habitats by human activities, and is often caused by deforestation.

The chapter is titled “Biological invasions in South Africa: A review of the status, impacts and research” and was published in the book “Biology and Control of Invasive Plants in Africa” which is edited by Phyllis Cole and Geoffrey K. Morris.

The book is a comprehensive look at invasive plants in Africa and was published as a joint effort by the Invasive Plant Atlas of New England and the Global Invasive Species Network. The book chapter on South Africa was written by Lutgardi Tyobeka, a master’s student at the University of Pretoria; Matthew C. Nxumalo, a senior lecturer at the University of KwaZulu-Natal; Gregory R. Davies, a research associate at the University of KwaZulu-Natal; and Mark J. Richardson, a research associate at the University of Cape Town.

In the chapter, the researchers looked at the number of scientific papers that have been published in peer-reviewed journals, books, theses and reports on biological invasions in South Africa. They found that from 1991 to 2015, 356 scientific papers were published. The researchers then looked at how many papers were published from 2001 to 2015, which is when South Africa’s National Biodiversity Institute and Working for Water program started invasive species research, and found that there were 239 papers published during that time period.

The program Working for Water started invasive species research in 2001 and has since trained staff from various government departments on how to identify and control invasive plants.

The researchers also looked at the number of papers that were published between 2011 and 2015, which is when the National Biodiversity Institute started the Invasive Species Programme, and found that there were 115 papers published during that time period.

The Invasive Species Programme has 9 nodes that are responsible for conducting research to prevent, detect and control invasive species, according to the National Biodiversity Institute.

In their chapter, the researchers found that there are many research gaps on biological invasions in South Africa, including the need for more research on invasive species that have not been prioritized, the need for more research on the impacts of invasive species, the need for more research on the control methods of invasive species and the need for more research on the social aspects of invasive species.

However, it is not clear how the vertical distribution of SOM across the silt plus clay (SPC) density classes differs with soil depth. We investigated the relationship between the vertical distribution of SOM and soil density for 0–20, 20–40, 40–60, and 60–100 cm soil depths from 12 temperate forest sites across the eastern United States. SOM content decreased exponentially with increasing SPC density for all soil depths, and the slope of the exponential equations were similar between soil depths, indicating similar SOM-SPC density relationships with depth. SOM concentrations within density classes increased with soil depth, suggesting that while the vertical distribution of SOM is primarily controlled by soil density, other factors that influence soil density also influence the location of SOM within the density classes with depth. This work contributes to our understanding of the distribution of SOM across different forest sites and soil depths and can be used to inform the development of models used to estimate carbon stocks in forest soils.

Here we describe the first SOM and C dataset from miombo woodland in Tanzania and explore the variability in soil organic carbon (SOC) and light fraction (Lf) stocks and density, and the soil organic matter (SOM) C concentration and C to N ratio. Soils were sampled across a gradient of tree cover (TC) ranging from 0-100% in the western Miombo woodland of Tanzania. SOC stocks increased with TC, but Lf and density increased to a peak at 50-75% TC and then declined. The SOM C concentration and C to N ratio were highest at 50% TC. Overall, the results suggest that the highest quality soils for carbon sequestration are found under closed stands of trees. These findings are important for the verification of carbon stocks in miombo woodlands, and for carbon accounting and forest management in sub-Saharan Africa.

samples.hyp:
Grazing animals can also help to restore damaged land, they add

By Edwin Mhede

Cutting down trees and grazing livestock on them can reduce the fertility of the soil, but careful management of trees and livestock can help restore damaged land, say scientists in Zambia.

Speaking at a media workshop in Lusaka, Zambian scientists said that trees play a vital role in soil fertility and that care should be taken when cutting them down.

“Careful management of trees and livestock is important for soil health,” said scientist Chipo Mawere. “When trees are cut, the stumps should be left in the ground to decay, to help add nutrients to the soil.”

Mawere and scientist Chipo Lukhele were speaking at a media workshop held in Lusaka, Zambia on 29 November 2019, organised by the International Centre for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT).

The scientists said that trees help to add nutrients and organic matter to the soil through their roots, leaves, branches, flowers, fruits, and back to the soil when they decay or are cut down.

“Trees also help to increase soil moisture levels and bind soil together, which is important for reducing soil erosion,” said Mawere.

But she said that overgrazing and indiscriminate cutting of trees can reduce the amount of organic carbon in the soil and other nutrients, which can reduce soil fertility and make the land less productive.

But she said that careful management of trees and livestock can help to increase the amount of organic carbon in the soil and other nutrients, which can improve soil health and increase productivity.

“Care should be taken when cutting down trees, and grazing animals can also help to restore damaged land,” said Mawere.

Lukhele said that trees help to increase the amount of nutrients in the soil through a process called nitrogen fixation, in which atmospheric nitrogen is converted to a form that is useful to plants.

“Nitrogen is an important nutrient for plant growth and organic carbon helps to make the soil more fertile,” she said.

CIAT’s media workshop in Zambia was part of a series of events to launch a new regional initiative — the Africa Soil Information System (ASIS), which will improve the understanding of soil conditions across 20 countries in eastern and southern Africa.

Funded by the Australian Government, ASIS will help policymakers and farmers make better decisions about soil management by providing them with access to better and more reliable soil information.

(Credit: E. Martin/University of Michigan)

Agricultural Research Service scientists in Athens, Georgia, and Ibadan, Nigeria, have proposed a new way to estimate soil organic carbon (SOC) using a single sample of soil.

Soil carbon is a key indicator of soil health and a critical component of climate change because soil stores large quantities of carbon, second only to the atmosphere.

Measuring soil carbon is difficult because soil is heterogeneous, varying from one location to another within a single field, and also because soil is a three-dimensional substance.

Previous attempts to estimate SOC have involved using models that require information about soil mineralogy, soil depth, climate, and other factors. However, few locations have the needed pedological and environmental data, and even in their presence, model estimates can be inaccurate.

The scientists, led by Agricultural Research Service (ARS) soil scientist Olubukola Ogunjesi of the Soil and Plant Nutrient Management Unit in Ibadan, propose a new way to estimate SOC using a method called cone of depression.

Cone of depression is a way to estimate the volume of soil and water that has been removed from the ground during drilling. This information is used to estimate the missing soil volume, which is then multiplied by soil bulk density to generate an estimate of SOC.

The new method was tested in a study of 68 soil profiles from across Nigeria. The new estimates were compared with SOC estimates derived from the collection and laboratory analysis of multiple soil cores from each soil profile. The new method was highly correlated with SOC derived from the more conventional method, and the error in the estimate was about 21 percent, which is lower than the errors associated with other methods that require more information.

The new method is described in a new study accepted for publication in Soil Science Society of America Journal. Ogunjesi and ARS soil scientist E. Martin, who is with the Soil and Plant Nutrient Management Unit in Athens, are co-authors of the study.

Their work was done in collaboration with scientists from the University of Ibadan and University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. The study was funded in part by ARS.

The ARS Soil and Plant Nutrient Management Unit is located at the University of Georgia.

The amount of nutrients and carbon in soil is determined by the amount of organic matter in the soil. 

Organic matter is made up of decaying plant and animal matter. The more organic matter in the soil, the more nutrients and carbon it has. 

Carbon is a key component of soil organic matter. 

Soil carbon is stored in the soil in three different ways:

1. As live plant roots – roots grow and decay, adding carbon to the soil

2. As dead roots and other organic matter in the soil – this organic matter breaks down and adds carbon to the soil

3. As microorganisms break down plant and organic matter – microorganisms (such as bacteria and fungi) break down plant and organic matter, which puts carbon into the soil.

This means that to increase the amount of carbon in the soil, you need to put carbon into the soil. 

You can do this by:

1. Planting trees and other crops that grow back every year

2. Leaving crop residue in the field after harvest

3. Using cover crops – cover crops are crops that grow quickly, and are then tilled back into the soil

4. Reducing or avoiding tillage

5. Using conservation agriculture practices

6. Using organic fertilizers

7. Using biochar

8. Stopping soil erosion – the more soil you can protect from erosion, the more carbon it has

9. Stopping soil compaction – the more soil can be protected from compaction, the more space is available for carbon

10. Stopping soil disturbance – the less soil is disturbed, the more carbon is stored in soil

The test can be used to compare soil health over time or to compare soil health within a field or farm. The test can also be used to calculate other indicators, such as the soil organic carbon to clay ratio, which can help predict the impact of management practices on soil health.
