The project aims to contribute to the resilience and sustainable production of pulse crops in Ethiopia by strengthening the capacity of the All Ethiopia Farmers Federation (AEFF) and the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) to improve chickpea quality and quantity through innovation platform approach. The specific objectives are:
1. To establish a multi-stakeholder platform for chickpea in Ethiopia
2. To evaluate the impact of the innovation platform on the productivity of chickpea
3. To strengthen the capacity of the AEFF and the EIAR on the use of innovation platforms in the Ethiopian agriculture.

The expected outcomes of the project are:
1. Multi-stakeholder platforms established and functional for sustainable production of chickpea in Ethiopia
2. Improved capacity of the AEFF and the EIAR to promote sustainable production of chickpea through innovation platforms
3. Increased productivity of chickpea in Ethiopia.

This project is aligned with the Ethiopian Agricultural Transformation and the Africa Green Revolution (AGRA) programs. It is also in line with the Ethiopian Government’s Agricultural Sector Development Program (ASDP II) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

The project will be implemented in three regions in Ethiopia, namely Tigray, Amhara and Oromia where chickpea is widely grown. The project will be implemented at woreda (district) level, in 10 woredas, namely Enderta, Tapelda, Antsoki, Abergelle, and Nifaas Mawcha in Tigray region; Dela, Wagara, and Guba in Amhara region; and Fantaallee and Boosat in Oromia region.

The project will be implemented by the International Potato Center (CIP) in collaboration with the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR), the All Ethiopia Farmers Federation (AEFF), the International Center for Insect Physiology and Ecology (ICIPE), and the University of California Davis (UCD). The total duration of the project is 36 months, including an 18-month planning and implementation period and a 6-month period for project closure.

It aims at facilitating the adoption of the improved technologies by the farmers and other stakeholders in the value chain. The Secretariat provides technical and financial management support to the Platform and its activities.

samples.hyp:
A SARS-CoV-2 lineage A variant (A.23.1) with altered spike has emerged and is dominating the current Uganda epidemic

  • Published on 26 January 2022
  • Last updated on 26 January 2022
  • Type: Article
  • DOI: 10.1101/2022.01.25.22269561

The emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants has been observed globally since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. In Uganda, the epidemic was dominated by the B.1.1.7 (Alpha) variant since late 2021. In this paper, we report the identification of a different SARS-CoV-2 lineage A variant (A.23.1) with an altered spike protein. The A.23.1 variant was detected in 73.3% of 107 samples collected from COVID-19 patients in Kampala between Nov 1st and Dec 17th, 2021. The A.23.1 spike protein has two amino acid changes, G75V and I85V, both located in the receptor-binding domain (RBD). The G75V mutation has been reported for the first time in the A.23 lineage. The in vitro binding of the A.23.1 RBD to human ACE2 receptors was not significantly different from that of the B.1.1.7 (Alpha) or B.1.617.2 (Delta) variants. However, the RBD of the A.23.1 variant showed reduced binding to the ACE2 receptors of African non-human primates (NHPs), compared to the B.1.1.7 and B.1.617.2 variants. Our findings suggest that the A.23.1 variant might have a reduced transmissibility in African NHPs, potentially making it less fit for continued transmission in this population. The reduced binding to African NHPs ACE2 receptors might also affect the infectivity of the A.23.1 variant in other primates or even in humans living in Uganda. Further studies are needed to better understand the impact of the A.23.1 variant in Uganda and other African countries.

Uganda is a landlocked country in East Africa with a population of ~48 million and only 44,000 total beds in the country’s health care system (0.09 per 1000 population). The country has been hard hit by the COVID-19 pandemic with > 115,000 confirmed cases and 3,000 deaths. However, underreporting is significant and the true burden of disease is estimated to be 10-20 times the reported numbers. The country is currently experiencing a 3rd wave of infections with the B.1.617.2 (Delta) variant as the predominant strain. Here, we describe a genomic surveillance system that has been in place since July 2020 and has sequenced > 6,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Uganda. The system combines a national public health laboratory with sequencing capacity and works in coordination with a number of partners including, but not limited to, the Uganda Virus Research Institute, other local laboratories, and international partners such as the Global Virome Project. The system provides real-time whole genome data on variants of SARS-CoV-2 and allows for rapid characterization of epidemiological and phylogenetic trends. The system also provides opportunities for training in genomic surveillance in the African context. The system is openly shared with the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID) and data are deposited to NCBI BioProject PRN PRN910596.

# Researchers report on SARS-CoV-2 variant evolution in Uganda

Posted by on

The researchers, led by Ira M. Longini of the University of Florida, used a mathematical model to estimate the growth rate of the B.1.1.28 (VUI-21MAY-01) variant in Uganda and the time it would take for the variant to become the dominant strain. They found that the variant is currently increasing 1.7-fold per week and would become the dominant variant in the country within 2–4 months.

The researchers also used their model to estimate the effectiveness of several public health interventions, including increasing the number of vaccine doses administered per week, improving public masking compliance, and reducing social contact by 50%. They found that increasing the number of vaccine doses administered per week from 300,000 to 1,000,000 would reduce the time it would take for the B.1.1.28 variant to become dominant by 90%. Improving masking compliance from 20% to 60% and reducing social contact by 50% would each reduce the time it would take for the variant to become dominant by 32–59 days.

The study provides important insights into the spread of the B.1.1.28 variant in Uganda and highlights the effectiveness of public health interventions in mitigating the spread of the variant. The findings also emphasize the need for continued surveillance and monitoring of SARS-CoV-2 variants in the country.

Scientists name variants with letters of the Greek alphabet to indicate their order of appearance in a given year.

A Feminist Theorist Takes On the Classic Article That Will Not Die

In 1972, a psychology professor published a landmark article titled “Women Are Better Than Men at Reading Faces.” The research went viral, became the subject of a popular podcast, and was recently the basis for a viral Twitter thread and a fierce debate about whether women really are better than men at determining people’s emotions. The research has been cited as evidence of women’s superiority in a wide range of real-world situations, including employment, relationships, and parenting. It has also been used to argue that women are better at making decisions that involve caring for others.

The research has been widely cited, in large part because it seemingly confirms people’s biases and beliefs about gender. But the research is deeply flawed. It suffers from serious methodological issues, which were obscured by questionable reporting in the original article. After the research went viral, a group of feminist researchers set out to replicate the study. Their replication efforts failed to replicate the effects, and they published a new study that included a detailed analysis of the flaws in the original study.

This article tells the story of that replication attempt, and features an interview with lead author Lila Leibovich.

In 2018, the Center for Health and Human Rights at Harvard University and the International Center for Research on Women collaborated on a research project to document the reasons why women in Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya support FGM/C, and the circumstances that lead to its continuation.

The project utilized a qualitative case study design with in-depth interviews and focus group discussions in each country with key stakeholders, including women who practice FGM/C, health care providers, and community and religious leaders. The research aimed to understand how FGM/C is embedded in social norms, cultural practices, and economic and social circumstances that vary by country and region.

The research found that FGM/C is part of a larger social construction that shapes gender norms and roles. While FGM/C is a key part, it is one part among many that are difficult to change in isolation. The research also found that the social and economic context that supports the continuation of FGM/C cutting has deep roots and is shaped by a combination of economic, social, and cultural factors. However, the evidence on the impact of their communication and information sharing is limited. This study assessed the impact of a training programme for health workers in primary health care centres in Somalia on their communication with girls and women about FGM/C. The study used a quasi-experimental design with a pre-test, post-test and 6-month follow-up. Qualitative semi-structured interviews were conducted with girls and women attending the health centres. The outcome indicators were knowledge, number of girls and women reached and prevalence of FGM/C practice. A total of 1,263 girls and women were reached by 29 health workers in two regions in Somalia. Health workers reported that they had discussed FGM/C with girls and women, and girls and women reported being counselled by health workers. There was a significant increase in knowledge of the health risks of FGM/C among girls and women who had been counselled by health workers. The number of girls and women counselled and the extent of travel to reach them increased significantly. The prevalence of FGM/C did not change significantly. Health workers in Somalia play an important role in the continuation of FGM/C. Training of health workers in communication skills and provision of accurate information on the negative health effects of FGM/C is important to change acceptability of FGM/C and ultimately reduce its practice.

To stop female genital mutilation, we first need to understand why it’s happening

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines female genital mutilation (FGM) as any procedure that involves partial or total removal of the external female genitalia, or any other injury to the female genital organs for non-medical purposes. This harmful practice is most commonly performed on girls aged between four and 14 years, and sometimes on infants and women. The WHO estimates that 200 million girls and women alive today have undergone FGM, and that 44 million more will be cut by 2030.

FGM is a deeply ingrained cultural practice that can be challenging to change. It is often seen as a necessary step to prepare girls for adulthood, and to ensure their chastity. Some communities believe that FGM is a religious obligation, or is needed for cultural or hygienic reasons. Others believe that it brings status and prestige, or that it is essential for future sexual relationships to be comfortable and enjoyable.

The practice of FGM has been banned in Somalia since 1973, and in Egypt since 2008, but it continues to be performed in both countries. In Somalia, the ban was not enforced due to the lack of a central government, and in Egypt, the ban was not widely known or understood. In both countries, FGM is often performed in secret, and the consequences for those who are caught performing the procedure are often minor.

In order to stop FGM, we need to understand why it is still being performed. We need to address the underlying cultural and social factors that support the practice. This means challenging harmful norms and traditions, and promoting positive alternatives. It also means providing accurate information and education about the risks and consequences of FGM.

There are many organizations and individuals working to end FGM. These include the United Nations, the World Health Organization, NGOs, and local community leaders. These groups are working to raise awareness about FGM, to provide support and services to those affected by FGM, and to advocate for policy change.

Ending FGM is a complex and challenging task, but it is possible. By understanding the reasons why FGM is still being performed, and by working together to address the underlying causes, we can help to ensure that this harmful practice is finally brought to an end.

samples.hyp:
The study was conducted to determine the sodium metavanadate (NaVO3) subchronic toxicity in male African giant rats (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840). Ten rats were used in the control group and 15 rats were used in the treatment group. The treatment group was administered NaVO3 at 150 mg/kg body weight in drinking water for 30 days. Results showed significant (P < 0.05) increase in body weight of the treatment group when compared to the control group. Significant (P < 0.05) decrease in testosterone level was observed in the treatment group. Histopathological examination of the testis of treated rats showed germ cell apoptosis and abnormal sperm morphophenotypes. Electron microscopic studies revealed ultrastructural changes in the testis of treated rats. These changes include; loss of spermatids at different stages, presence of apoptotic bodies, vacuolation and reduction in size of seminiferous tubules, reduction in size of mitochondria, disruption of fertility vacuoles, loss of microvilli in Sertoli cells and presence of apoptotic bodies in the interstitial spaces. The study showed that NaVO3 induced reproductive toxicity in male African giant rats. The reproductive toxicity may be as a result of decrease in testosterone level and the subsequent changes in the testis. The loss of germ cells could be as a result of the direct effect of NaVO3 on the germ cells and/or indirect effect via Sertoli cells. The abnormal sperm morphophenotypes could be as a result of the changes in the Sertoli cells, which have important supportive role for spermatogenesis. In conclusion, NaVO3 induced reproductive toxicity, which may be as a result of the decrease in testosterone level and the subsequent changes in the testis.

The results of the sperm analysis showed that the sperm motility of the rats treated with 50 mg/kg of SMV was significantly decreased (p < 0.0001). The head and tail movements of the sperm were also significantly decreased (p < 0.0001 and p < 0.0001, respectively). The sperm viability, on the other hand, was significantly increased in the rats treated with 10 mg/kg of SMV (p < 0.0001). The levels of testicular oxidative stress markers, including lipid peroxidation and reactive oxygen species, were significantly increased in the rats treated with 50 mg/kg of SMV (p < 0.0001 and p < 0.0001, respectively). The activities of the testicular antioxidant enzymes, superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase, were significantly decreased in the rats treated with 50 mg/kg of SMV (p < 0.0001 and p < 0.0001, respectively). The levels of testicular testosterone and luteinizing hormone were significantly decreased in the rats treated with 50 mg/kg of SMV (p < 0.0001 and p < 0.0001, respectively). The results of the histological analysis showed that the testicular tissue of the rats treated with 50 mg/kg of SMV was significantly damaged (p < 0.0001). The seminiferous tubules of the rats treated with 50 mg/kg of SMV were significantly atrophied (p < 0.0001). The present study demonstrated that SMV has adverse effects on the reproductive system of male African giant rats, and the no observed adverse effect level for SMV on male reproductive toxicity is estimated to be 10 mg/kg body weight.

Serum luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and testosterone (T) levels were decreased (P < 0.05) in rats treated with SMV compared to vehicle-treated rats. SMV-treated rats had a significantly (P < 0.05) higher serum progesterone level than vehicle controls. The total sperm count, forward motility and viability were significantly (P < 0.05) lower in SMV-treated rats than in vehicle-treated rats. The percentage of normal sperm was significantly (P < 0.05) lower in SMV-treated rats compared to vehicle controls. The percentage of coiled sperm was significantly (P < 0.05) higher in SMV-treated rats than in vehicle-treated rats. The main ultrastructural changes in the testis were the degenerative changes in the seminiferous epithelium. These changes included the degeneration of spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids and spermatozoa. The most prominent change was the appearance of large, round, dark mitochondria in the spermatogonia.

The results of the present study indicate that treatment with SMV results in a decline in reproductive hormone levels, sperm quality and quantity as well as ultrastructural changes in the testis. The decrease in reproductive hormone levels as indicated by the decreased FSH, LH and T levels in the present study is in agreement with the findings of other studies where treatment with SMV (Forsgren et al., 2004; van der Waaij et al., 2005) and other antiandrogens (Ergazzi et al., 2009) resulted in decreased levels of reproductive hormones. The decreased levels of reproductive hormones could result in a decline in reproductive capacity.

The study concluded that the oral SMV treatment induced apoptosis in testes and epididymis of male rats. This study is the first to report the apoptotic effect of SMV in male reproductive system. The study was supported by the College of Science and Liberal Arts, SNU.

The study was conducted by Dr. Myoung Keun Suh and his research team from the Department of Biological Sciences and the Institute of Genetic Medicine, SNU. The team analyzed the apoptotic effect of SMV in the male reproductive system of rats. Dr. Suh said, “SMV is a widely used drug in Korea. The male reproductive system is very sensitive to the drug, so we examined the toxic effect of SMV in the male reproductive system.” He added, “apoptosis is a type of cell death that occurs in living organisms. It is a programmed cell death and occurs when an organism is developing. The death helps organisms to control the development of a tissue or organ, and it helps the body eliminate old or damaged cells.”

Dr. Suh and his team found that the oral treatment of SMV induced apoptosis in a dose-dependent manner in the testes and epididymis of male rats. They also discovered that SMV treatment group showed statistically decreased sperm motility and mass activity with increased percentage of abnormal morphophenotypes of spermatozoa and upregulation of P53 immunopositive cell in the cauda epididymis.

Dr. Suh said, “we revealed the apoptotic effect of SMV in the male reproductive system for the first time. This result will be helpful to identify the cause of side effects of SMV in clinical use.” He further said, “we will keep working to examine the toxic effect of drugs in the male reproductive system.”

samples.hyp:
The Independent / Dec 19, 2006

E-mail this story

Industrial pollution may leave women unable to have children, according to researchers.

Scientists in Sweden have found that rats exposed to metal fumes from car factories and steelworks are less fertile.

The study, by experts at the Umea University, examined the impact of airborne pollutants on male rats from birth.

The animals were less fertile as adults and had lower levels of testosterone, researchers said.

The findings could have serious implications for humans, particularly in countries such as the UK which have a high level of industrial activity, the journal Environmental Health Perspectives reported.

The scientists said that the most likely culprit was nickel, a metal found in car exhaust fumes and from burning fossil fuels.

"Our hypothesis was that the metals were affecting the male reproductive system via the immune system," said one of the researchers, Dr. Royal Mostofsky.

"This was a common-sense approach. We know that one of the functions of the immune system is to discriminate the body's own cells from foreign cells."

The study established that the rats' immune systems were recognising the metal fumes as foreign, and were attacking them. In doing so, they accidentally attacked the rats' own cells, leaving them less fertile.

Mostofsky said that the findings suggested that human exposure to low levels of pollutants over a long period of time could affect their fertility.

"Although the effects we saw in rats occurred at a high level of exposure, there are many more humans living and working in places where the levels of pollutants are much higher," he said.

"It's not that we are saying people should move out of these areas or that there needs to be a change in government policy. But I think these results should be taken into account when people are making decisions."

The present study was designed to investigate the effects of vanadium (V) on the reproductive system of male rats. Materials and Methods. A total of 25 male rats were randomly divided into five groups. Groups 1 to 4 received oral V at doses of 1, 2, and 4 mg/kg body weight in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) for 90 successive days, respectively, and group 5 received DMSO only and served as a negative control. At the end of the experimental period, the rats were euthanized, and their reproductive systems were removed, processed, and analyzed. Results. The results of this study showed a significant decrease in body weight of male rats treated with V in a dose-dependent manner. Testes weight was significantly reduced in rats treated with 4 mg/kg V. Also, V induced a significant decrease in the sperm count, motility, and viability of rats treated with 4 mg/kg. In addition, V caused a significant increase in the levels of lactic acid dehydrogenase (LDH) and testosterone with a significant decrease in the level of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Conclusion. These findings suggest that long-term treatment with high doses of V may produce adverse effects on the male reproductive system. More research is needed to explore the molecular mechanisms of action of V on the male reproductive system.

samples.ref: Ìlò ajẹmáṣà àwọn Ewéko Ọgbà-etílé ní àwọn Àdúgbò Ìjímìjí ní Àríwá-Ìwọ̀-oorùn Ethiopia.
samples.hyp:
The aim of this study was to identify the homegarden plant species in the community and to assess the cultural importance of these species. A total of 61 homegarden plant species from 37 families were recorded in the homegarden. The cultural importance index (CII) was calculated for all species and the results showed that the species are used in different cultural activities to different extents. The three most important categories were food, medicine, and craft. The CII was used to calculate the cultural importance of the species in four different ecosystems. The results showed that the cultural use of homegarden plants was higher in the traditional bushland compared to the other ecosystems. The results also showed that the cultural use of homegarden plants was not dependent on the use value of the plants. The results of this study could be used in in-situ conservation programs of the homegarden plant species in Ethiopia.

samples.hyp:
This study aims at assessing the floristic composition of homegardens in the district, and to explore its spatial variation. In addition, it explores the relationship between the floristic composition and main land uses, and the variation of homegardens in the district. Descriptive statistics, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), Shannon diversity index, global similarity, and nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) were used to analyze the data.
A total of 66 homegardens in 13 villages within 10 sampling sites were selected randomly. In each garden, all woody and herbaceous plants were identified, and their abundance was estimated.
Results showed that the homegarden owners in the study area used 59 plant species as boundary fences, 64 species as a source of firewood, 45 species for construction works, 33 species for roof thatching, 25 species for house flooring, 23 species for tool handles, 21 species for house posts, 20 species for furniture making, 17 species for fencing their homestead, 16 species for food production, 14 species for traditional medicine, 13 species for roofing tiles, 12 species for charcoal production, and 10 species for animal fodder. The most common plant families in homegardens were Poaceae, Rosaceae, Rubiaceae, and Fabaceae. The homegardens in the study area had high species diversity (H′=1.89). The average global similarity among the homegardens was 46.0%, and the average dissimilarity was 54.0%. MANOVA results showed a statistically significant difference in the composition of homegardens among the sampling sites (P<0.001). The NMDS analysis showed a distinct separation between the floristic assemblages of the southern and northern sampling sites.
The study also revealed that human population density, area of cultivated land, and percentage of forested and degraded lands influenced the variation of homegardens in the study area. In addition, the major land uses in the study area were farming, wood/grazing land, forest/woodland, human settlement, and grassland.
This is the first study that assessed the variation of homegardens in the Gozamin district of Ethiopia. The study revealed that the homegardens in the district had high species diversity, and their floristic composition was influenced by human population density, percentage of forested and degraded lands, and area of cultivated land.

Homegardens are a significant land use across the globe, particularly in Africa, yet relatively little is known about their composition and significance. This research is intended to address this knowledge gap. To accomplish this, we are collecting data in four West African countries (Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal, Benin) and in two West African diaspora cities in the United States (Washington, DC and Atlanta, GA). In each country and city, we are studying homegardens in two regions: rural and urban. The data we collect includes plant species present, as well as data on management, products, services, and economic importance. We are also collecting ethnographic data (photographs, video, and interviews) to help better understand the context of the gardens and the cultures in which they occur. The researchers also want to examine whether some of the garden plants have already been introduced to Ethiopia as a result of immigration from other parts of the world where they normally occur.

In the United States, for example, a community garden can be a safe space for refugees to grow the food from their homeland, according to researchers from Rutgers University in New Jersey.

Now, researchers from the University of Georgia have found that community gardens can also be a source of healthy food for people experiencing food insecurity.

The study, published online April 21 in the Journal of Food Security, defines food insecurity as a “state in which people, for financial or social reasons, are unable to access food considered sufficient by national and international standards.”

For the research, the team used data from the 2018 National Survey of Fishing, Hunting and Wildlife Associated Recreation. This included information from 1,983 gardeners who maintained at least one garden in the past 12 months. The data focused on 2017, a year without a major natural disaster or other significant event that would impact food availability.

The researchers found that 5% of gardeners reported they did not have enough food to consistently afford a healthy diet for all household members. Of these gardeners, 6% reported their community garden was a source of food.

Gardeners who identified as Hispanic and Latino, and those who reported their households made less than $50,000 a year, were more likely to report their community garden was a source of food.

“Community gardens have been found to have positive impacts on social capital, health, mental health, nutrition and physical activity,” the researchers wrote in a university press release.

“Health and nutrition outcomes were improved among individuals and social groups that had more frequent access to the gardens, suggesting that accessibility is an important design element,” they added.

The researchers noted that community garden programs are a promising strategy to address food insecurity and other food problems, but their findings also suggest that food insecurity is a complex social problem that requires multiple strategies to address.

“Future research should continue to explore the connections between community gardens and food security, and should also explore the full range of factors that may influence the food security benefits of community gardens,” the researchers concluded.
